# A Poison Tree analysis

A Poison Tree — William Blake (1794)

Blake traces anger from honest expression to secret cultivation, deceit, and revenge.

Full text from [A Poison Tree](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/A_Poison_Tree). Public domain in the US (First published in Songs of Experience in 1794; public domain in the United States.).

## Summary

The speaker’s anger toward a friend ends when expressed, but anger toward a foe grows when concealed. It becomes a tree fed by fear, tears, smiles, and deceit.

```
I was angry with my friend;
I told my wrath, my wrath did end.
I was angry with my foe:
```

A bright apple draws the foe into the garden, and the speaker greets the result with disturbing pleasure.[2]

## Meaning and interpretation

The poem warns that secrecy changes anger into a cultivated plan. The speaker is morally implicated because false friendliness sustains the resentment.[2]

```
And it grew both day and night.
Till it bore an apple bright.
```

The attractive fruit disguises the poison within and recalls the forbidden fruit of Genesis.

## Themes

### Communication and anger

The opening parallelism presents expression as release and silence as growth.

### Secrecy and hypocrisy

```
And I sunned it with smiles,
And with soft deceitful wiles.
```

The speaker performs friendliness while nurturing hostility.

### Revenge

```
In the morning glad I see
My foe outstretched beneath the tree.
```

The speaker’s gladness makes the ending morally unsettling rather than triumphant.

## Form and meter

Four quatrains use short, strongly stressed lines and paired end rhymes. The simple, nursery-rhyme surface contrasts with the subject of deception and death.[3]

Repeated syntax makes the poem a compact moral experiment: telling anger ends it, while concealment grows it.

## Literary devices

### Extended metaphor

```
And I waterd it in fears,
Night & morning with my tears:
```

Wrath becomes a tree that can be deliberately cultivated.

### Biblical symbolism

```
Till it bore an apple bright.
And my foe beheld it shine,
```

Garden, tree, fruit, and trespass echo Eden while reversing its moral pattern.

### Antithesis

The nearly identical friend and foe sentences show how one small change—telling or not telling—produces opposite consequences.

## Historical context

Blake published the poem in Songs of Experience (1794), paired with Songs of Innocence under the subtitle “Two Contrary States of the Human Soul.” The manuscript title “Christian Forbearance” sharpens the irony of polite concealment.[4]

```
When the night had veild the pole;
In the morning glad I see
```

The garden imagery places a private quarrel inside biblical language about temptation and the Fall.

## What critics say

> “The poem uses an extended metaphor to describe the speaker’s anger as growing into a tree that bears poisonous apples.”
>
> — [LitCharts](https://www.litcharts.com/poetry/william-blake/a-poison-tree)

> “In deceptively simple language with an almost nursery-rhyme quality.”
>
> — [LitCharts](https://www.litcharts.com/poetry/william-blake/a-poison-tree)

## Common questions

### What is the main meaning?

Hidden anger nurtured through fear and deceit can become destructive, unlike anger openly expressed.

### What does the apple symbolize?

It is an attractive but poisonous product of resentment and an allusion to forbidden fruit.

### What form does it use?

Four quatrains with paired rhymes create a memorable nursery-rhyme surface.

## References

- [Wikisource](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/A_Poison_Tree)

- [LitCharts](https://www.litcharts.com/poetry/william-blake/a-poison-tree)

- [LitCharts](https://www.litcharts.com/poetry/william-blake/a-poison-tree)

- [Wikisource](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/A_Poison_Tree)

## Open the editor

Write with this poem’s meter in the editor: https://lyriic.com/write/common-meter

# A Thing of Beauty Is a Joy Forever analysis

A Thing of Beauty Is a Joy Forever — John Keats (1818)

Keats’s opening to Endymion argues that beauty gives lasting comfort in a difficult world.

Full text from [Endymion: A Poetic Romance](https://gutenberg.org/files/24280/24280-h/24280-h.htm). Public domain in the US (Endymion was first published in 1818; public domain in the United States.).

## Summary

Keats begins with the claim that beauty grows in value and provides a quiet refuge. He then catalogs natural forms, stories, and imagined memorials before ending with an inexhaustible fountain.

```
A thing of beauty is a joy for ever:
Its loveliness increases; it will never
Pass into nothingness;
```

The passage answers gloomy experience with beauty’s sustaining force.[2]

## Meaning and interpretation

Beauty does not deny suffering; it is offered as a way to endure it. The bower, sleep, health, and quiet breathing make consolation bodily.[2]

```
Some shape of beauty moves away the pall
From our dark spirits.
```

The catalogue expands from nature to art, suggesting that imagination also nourishes life.

## Themes

### Beauty as consolation

Beauty shelters people from despondence and binds them to continued existence.

### Nature and renewal

```
Such the sun, the moon,
Trees old, and young, sprouting a shady boon
```

Seasonal forms become recurring evidence that loveliness can renew itself.

### Art and imagination

```
All lovely tales that we have heard or read;
An endless fountain of immortal drink,
```

Stories join natural beauty as a durable source of imaginative nourishment.

## Form and meter

The opening is written in heroic couplets, predominantly iambic pentameter, with an AABB pattern.[3]

Enjambment lets syntax run across couplets, creating a flowing movement that suits the fountain image.

## Literary devices

### Metaphor

```
A flowery band to bind us to the earth,
Spite of despondence,
```

Beauty becomes a binding force that keeps people connected to life.

### Catalogue

The list moves from sun and moon through flowers and streams to stories, broadening the meaning of beauty.

### Sensory imagery

```
A bower quiet for us, and a sleep
Full of sweet dreams, and health, and quiet breathing.
```

Shelter, sleep, and breath make aesthetic consolation tangible.

## Historical context

Endymion: A Poetic Romance was published in 1818 as a long narrative based on the myth of Endymion and Cynthia. This opening proem states the values that guide the romance.[4]

```
And such too is the grandeur of the dooms
We have imagined for the mighty dead;
```

The passage’s early reception was harsh, but its account of beauty became one of Keats’s most quoted arguments.

## What critics say

> “The beauties of nature and art offer humanity not just a brief holiday from the world's troubles, but lasting consolation, even reason to go on living.”
>
> — [LitCharts](https://www.litcharts.com/poetry/john-keats/a-thing-of-beauty-is-a-joy-for-ever-from-endymion)

> “Keats’s opening uses rhyming couplets and frequent enjambment.”
>
> — [LitCharts](https://www.litcharts.com/poetry/john-keats/a-thing-of-beauty-is-a-joy-for-ever-from-endymion)

## Common questions

### What does the opening mean?

Genuine beauty continues to give pleasure and consolation, helping people endure suffering.

### What are the main themes?

Beauty as consolation, nature’s renewal, imagination, art, and mortality.

### What form does it use?

It uses heroic couplets in predominantly iambic pentameter with frequent enjambment.

## References

- [Project Gutenberg](https://gutenberg.org/files/24280/24280-h/24280-h.htm)

- [LitCharts](https://www.litcharts.com/poetry/john-keats/a-thing-of-beauty-is-a-joy-for-ever-from-endymion)

- [LitCharts](https://www.litcharts.com/poetry/john-keats/a-thing-of-beauty-is-a-joy-for-ever-from-endymion)

- [Project Gutenberg](https://gutenberg.org/files/24280/24280-h/24280-h.htm)

## Open the editor

Write with this poem’s meter in the editor: https://lyriic.com/write/iambic-pentameter

# A Valediction: Forbidding Mourning analysis

A Valediction: Forbidding Mourning — John Donne (1633)

Donne turns physical separation into an argument for spiritual love through gold, spheres, and a compass.

Full text from [A Valediction: Forbidding Mourning](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poems/44131/a-valediction-forbidding-mourning). Public domain in the US (First published posthumously in 1633; public domain in the United States.).

## Summary

The speaker asks his beloved to part quietly, contrasting their refined love with ordinary love that depends on physical presence. Two images then explain endurance: souls expand like beaten gold and resemble compass legs.

```
So let us melt, and make no noise,
No tear-floods, nor sigh-tempests move;
```

Distance becomes an expansion that still returns home.[2]

## Meaning and interpretation

The poem argues that mature love survives separation because it is grounded in mind and soul rather than only the senses.[2]

```
Our two souls therefore, which are one,
Though I must go, endure not yet
A breach, but an expansion,
```

The compass makes fidelity geometric: the beloved’s firmness gives the traveling speaker direction.

## Themes

### Spiritual love

A refined bond remains secure when eyes, lips, and hands are apart.

### Distance and connection

```
Like gold to airy thinness beat.
```

Separation stretches the relationship without breaking it.

### Constancy and return

```
Thy firmness makes my circle just,
And makes me end where I begun.
```

The fixed foot’s steadiness makes return possible.

## Form and meter

Nine quatrains use alternating rhyme. The lines are chiefly iambic tetrameter, with variations that preserve an argumentative speaking voice.[3]

Each stanza advances a comparison, culminating in the compass conceit across the final three stanzas.

## Literary devices

### Metaphysical conceit

```
As stiff twin compasses are two;
Thy soul, the fixed foot, makes no show
```

The surprising mechanical comparison makes emotional fidelity visible as coordinated motion.

### Simile

Beaten gold and the compass offer physical models for a bond that expands but does not break.

### Antithesis

```
Moving of th' earth brings harms and fears,
But trepidation of the spheres,
```

Earthly disturbance and celestial movement prepare the contrast between ordinary and refined love.

## Historical context

The poem was probably written around 1611–12 for Donne’s wife before a journey and appeared in Songs and Sonnets in 1633. Its title frames a farewell while forbidding conventional public grief.[4]

```
Dull sublunary lovers' love
(Whose soul is sense) cannot admit
```

The vocabulary reflects Renaissance distinctions between earthly sensation and spiritual experience.

## What critics say

> “Valediction contains one of the most famous conceits in all of literature: that in which the speaker likens himself and his lover to two points of a draftsman’s compass.”
>
> — [SparkNotes](https://www.sparknotes.com/poetry/a-valediction-forbidding-mourning/poetic-devices/)

> “The speaker sustains this conceit throughout the poem’s final three stanzas.”
>
> — [SparkNotes](https://www.sparknotes.com/poetry/a-valediction-forbidding-mourning/poetic-devices/)

## Common questions

### What is the main meaning?

A spiritually grounded love can survive physical separation without dramatic mourning.

### What does the compass conceit mean?

The beloved is the fixed foot; the traveling speaker remains connected and returns home.

### What form and meter does it use?

Nine quatrains with alternating rhyme and chiefly iambic tetrameter.

## References

- [Poetry Foundation](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poems/44131/a-valediction-forbidding-mourning)

- [SparkNotes](https://www.sparknotes.com/poetry/a-valediction-forbidding-mourning/poetic-devices/)

- [Poetry Foundation](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poems/44131/a-valediction-forbidding-mourning)

- [SparkNotes](https://www.sparknotes.com/poetry/a-valediction-forbidding-mourning/poetic-devices/)

## Open the editor

Write with this poem’s meter in the editor: https://lyriic.com/write/iambic-tetrameter

# Acquainted with the Night analysis

Acquainted with the Night — Robert Frost (1928)

Frost uses a rainy city walk, interlocking rhyme, and circular repetition to explore solitude.

Full text from [Acquainted with the Night](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poems/47548/acquainted-with-the-night). Public domain in the US (First published in 1928; public domain under the project’s US screening policy.).

## Summary

A first-person speaker repeatedly walks through a rainy city, passing a watchman and hearing a distant cry. A high clock says the time is neither wrong nor right.

```
I have been one acquainted with the night.
I have walked out in rain—and back in rain.
I have outwalked the furthest city light.
```

The identical opening and closing line makes the journey circular and unresolved.[2]

## Meaning and interpretation

Night is both setting and figure for inward loneliness. The speaker is surrounded by houses and possible voices yet remains separate from human contact.[2]

```
But not to call me back or say good-bye;
And further still at an unearthly height,
```

“Acquainted” suggests familiarity without intimacy: the speaker knows darkness through repetition but does not master it.

## Themes

### Solitude

Loneliness occurs within a populated city, not only in an empty landscape.

### Night and inward experience

```
I have looked down the saddest city lane.
I have passed by the watchman on his beat
```

The urban route reflects the speaker’s interior state.

### Time and uncertainty

```
Proclaimed the time was neither wrong nor right.
```

The clock offers judgment without resolution.

## Form and meter

The 14-line poem is a terza-rima sonnet: four tercets followed by a couplet, with interlocking rhyme and predominantly iambic pentameter.[3]

Repeated “I have” creates a measured pulse like recurring footsteps; the final repetition returns the speaker to his condition.

## Literary devices

### Repetition

```
I have been one acquainted with the night.
```

The framing line makes solitude habitual and circular.

### Personification

The luminary clock proclaims a judgment, but its words preserve ambiguity rather than answering the speaker.

### Auditory imagery

```
When far away an interrupted cry
Came over houses from another street,
```

Sound briefly connects separate lives, then fails to summon the speaker.

## Historical context

The poem appeared in 1928 in West-Running Brook after publication in the Virginia Quarterly Review. Its urban setting distinguishes it from Frost’s better-known rural lyrics.[4]

```
One luminary clock against the sky
Proclaimed the time was neither wrong nor right.
```

A constructed lyric voice, rather than a direct autobiography, carries the poem’s uncertainty.

## What critics say

> “Acquainted with the Night is a terza rima sonnet with the traditional 14 lines and ending couplet.”
>
> — [LitCharts](https://www.litcharts.com/poetry/robert-frost/acquainted-with-the-night)

> “Each line is also written using iambic pentameter.”
>
> — [LitCharts](https://www.litcharts.com/poetry/robert-frost/acquainted-with-the-night)

## Common questions

### What is the main meaning?

The poem presents repeated night walking as a figure for loneliness, inward reflection, and uncertainty.

### What are the themes?

Solitude, urban isolation, night, time, and unresolved judgment.

### What form does it use?

A terza-rima sonnet with four tercets, a closing couplet, and predominantly iambic pentameter.

## References

- [Poetry Foundation](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poems/47548/acquainted-with-the-night)

- [LitCharts](https://www.litcharts.com/poetry/robert-frost/acquainted-with-the-night)

- [LitCharts](https://www.litcharts.com/poetry/robert-frost/acquainted-with-the-night)

- [Poetry Foundation](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poems/47548/acquainted-with-the-night)

## Open the editor

Write with this poem’s meter in the editor: https://lyriic.com/write/iambic-pentameter

# All the World's a Stage analysis

All the World's a Stage — William Shakespeare (1623)

Jaques turns human life into a seven-part performance, from infancy to oblivion.

Full text from [As You Like It, Act II, Scene VII](https://poets.org/poem/you-it-act-ii-scene-vii-all-worlds-stage). Public domain in the US (The speech appears in the 1623 First Folio; Shakespeare’s work is public domain.).

## Summary

Jaques answers Duke Senior’s theater image by comparing every person to an actor. Each person enters, performs several roles, and eventually exits.

```
All the world's a stage,
And all the men and women merely players;
They have their exits and their entrances,
```

The seven ages move from comic snapshots to bodily decline and oblivion.[2]

## Meaning and interpretation

The extended metaphor suggests that identity changes with social roles: schoolboy, lover, soldier, justice, and old man are performances as much as biological stages.[2]

```
Seeking the bubble reputation
Even in the cannon's mouth.
```

The final “sans” sequence strips away the senses and roles that earlier ages use to define a person.

## Themes

### Aging and mortality

```
Is second childishness and mere oblivion,
Sans teeth, sans eyes, sans taste, sans everything.
```

The return to dependence becomes a terrifying loss rather than a comforting cycle.

### Performance and identity

Stage vocabulary makes social identity legible as a succession of roles.

### Vanity and reputation

The soldier risks life for a reputation described as a fragile bubble.

## Form and meter

This dramatic monologue is written in mostly unrhymed iambic pentameter, or blank verse. Flexible stresses and occasional feminine endings keep the speech conversational.[3]

Seven stages give the speech a compressed plot, while the final repetitions create a falling cadence.

## Literary devices

### Extended metaphor

```
And one man in his time plays many parts,
His acts being seven ages.
```

Entrances and exits become birth and death; roles become life stages.

### Simile

```
And shining morning face, creeping like snail
Unwillingly to school.
```

The snail makes reluctance physical and comic.

### Anaphora

```
Sans teeth, sans eyes, sans taste, sans everything.
```

Repeated “sans” removes one capacity at a time until nothing remains.

## Historical context

As You Like It was written around 1598–1600 and published in the First Folio in 1623. The speech is spoken by the melancholy Jaques in Act II, Scene VII.[4]

```
This wide and universal theatre
Presents more woeful pageants than the scene
```

Jaques completes Duke Senior’s theater image and turns it into a darker philosophy of life.

## What critics say

> “This is the idea that Jaques takes as his starting point in his ‘seven ages of man’ speech.”
>
> — [Royal Shakespeare Company](https://www.rsc.org.uk/shakespeare-learning-zone/as-you-like-it/language/analysis)

> “A mixture of perfect iambic pentameter lines with lines containing feminine endings or even as many as thirteen syllables.”
>
> — [Royal Shakespeare Company](https://www.rsc.org.uk/shakespeare-learning-zone/as-you-like-it/language/analysis)

## Common questions

### What is the main meaning?

Life is presented as a sequence of changing roles that ends in old age, dependence, and death.

### What are the seven ages?

Infant, schoolboy, lover, soldier, justice, pantaloon, and second childishness with oblivion.

### What form does it use?

It is a dramatic monologue in mostly unrhymed iambic pentameter, or blank verse.

## References

- [Academy of American Poets](https://poets.org/poem/you-it-act-ii-scene-vii-all-worlds-stage)

- [Royal Shakespeare Company](https://www.rsc.org.uk/shakespeare-learning-zone/as-you-like-it/language/analysis)

- [Royal Shakespeare Company](https://www.rsc.org.uk/shakespeare-learning-zone/as-you-like-it/language/analysis)

- [Academy of American Poets](https://poets.org/poem/you-it-act-ii-scene-vii-all-worlds-stage)

## Open the editor

Write with this poem’s meter in the editor: https://lyriic.com/write/iambic-pentameter

# Awake! Young Men of England analysis

Awake! Young Men of England — George Orwell (1914)

This analysis examines how Orwell’s youthful wartime poem turns enlistment into a test of courage and loyalty.

Full text from [Awake! Young Men of England](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Awake!_Young_Men_of_England). Public domain in the US (Published in 1914, before the US public-domain cutoff.).

## Summary

The speaker addresses young English men during the opening months of the First World War and urges them to enlist. Animal emblems and blunt military language make recruitment sound like a test of character.

```
Awake! Oh you young men of England,
For if, when your Country’s in need,
You do not enlist by the thousand,
```

The final accusation turns patriotic pressure into public shame: refusing service is labeled cowardice.[3]

## Meaning and interpretation

The poem presents enlistment as a moral obligation rather than a choice. Its simplified heroic vocabulary leaves little room for fear, dissent, or conscientious objection.

```
You truly are cowards indeed.
```

The image of soldiers throwing away their lives briefly acknowledges sacrifice, but uses it to intensify the appeal rather than question the war.[2]

## Themes

### Patriotism and duty

Repeated appeals to England and “your Country” make national service the expected proof of belonging.

### Shame as persuasion

The closing couplet divides the audience into men who answer the call and those branded cowards.

### Heroic language and violence

```
The strength of the Lion,
The wisdom of Reynard the Fox
```

Fable-like symbols make modern violence sound energetic and uncomplicated.

## Form and meter

The poem uses three quatrains with alternating rhyme in each stanza. Its loose four-beat, ballad-like rhythm and short clauses suit public recitation.

The stanzas move from imagined strength, to danger and sacrifice, to a command. The repeated address gives the ending the sound of a slogan.

## Literary devices

### Direct address

```
Awake! Oh you young men of England
```

The imperative summons a public audience and makes each young man feel personally responsible.

### Animal symbolism

```
The strength of the Lion,
The wisdom of Reynard the Fox
```

The lion suggests courage and the fox cunning, a compact inventory of qualities desired in war.

### Metaphor

```
Oh! think of the War Lord’s mailed fist
```

The enemy becomes a striking armored hand, making an abstract threat bodily and immediate.

## Historical context

The poem appeared in the Henley and South Oxfordshire Standard on October 2, 1914, soon after Britain entered the First World War. Orwell was then eleven-year-old Eric Blair.[2]

The Orwell Foundation describes it as the energetic, romantic view of warfare of a child at the start of the war; its historical value lies partly in the contrast with Orwell’s mature political skepticism.[3]

## What critics say

> “the patriotic fervour of ‘Awake! Young Men of England’, published in the Henley & South Oxfordshire Standard on 2 October 1914”
>
> — D. J. Taylor, [The Orwell Society](https://orwellsociety.com/edition-of-orwells-poems-a-triumph/)

> “the energy and excitement of a child’s romantic view of warfare”
>
> — [The Orwell Foundation](https://www.orwellfoundation.com/uncategorized/fools-rush-in/)

## Common questions

### What is the poem’s meaning?

It urges young English men to enlist and uses patriotism and shame to frame service as moral duty.

### What are its themes?

Patriotism, masculine courage, recruitment, shame, and the gap between heroic language and wartime cost.

### What is its form?

Three rhymed quatrains in a loose, four-beat ballad-like rhythm.

## References

- [Wikisource](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Awake!_Young_Men_of_England)

- [D. J. Taylor, The Orwell Society](https://orwellsociety.com/edition-of-orwells-poems-a-triumph/)

- [The Orwell Foundation](https://www.orwellfoundation.com/uncategorized/fools-rush-in/)

- [D. J. Taylor, The Orwell Foundation](https://www.orwellfoundation.com/the-orwell-foundation/orwell/articles/d-j-taylor-orwells-poetry/)

## Open the editor

Write with this poem’s rhythm in the editor: https://lyriic.com/write

# Because I Could Not Stop for Death analysis

Because I Could Not Stop for Death — Emily Dickinson (1890)

Dickinson turns dying into a calm but unsettling carriage ride toward an uncertain eternity.

Full text from [Because I could not stop for Death](https://poets.org/poem/because-i-could-not-stop-death-479). Public domain in the US (First published posthumously in 1890, before the US public-domain cutoff.).

## Summary

Death courteously stops for the speaker, who enters a carriage with Death and Immortality. The journey passes children, grain, sunset, and finally a grave.[1]

```
Because I could not stop for Death—
He kindly stopped for me—
The Carriage held but just Ourselves—
```

Centuries later, the speaker still remembers first guessing that the horses were headed toward Eternity.

## Meaning and interpretation

Polite words such as “kindly” and “Civility” make death sound like a genteel visit, but the speaker also surrenders work, leisure, clothing, and control.

```
We paused before a House that seemed
A Swelling of the Ground—
The Roof was scarcely visible—
```

The ending is directional rather than conclusive: Eternity remains a destination the poem approaches without explaining.[2]

## Themes

### Death as social encounter

Personified Death behaves like a patient gentleman caller, making dying familiar while leaving the speaker’s surrender unsettling.

### Stages of life

```
We passed the School, where Children strove
At Recess—in the Ring—
We passed the Fields of Gazing Grain—
```

School, grain, and sunset compress childhood, maturity, and decline into one route.

### Immortality and uncertainty

Immortality rides silently in the carriage; its presence suggests survival without proving what that survival means.

## Form and meter

Six quatrains broadly follow common meter, alternating iambic tetrameter and trimeter. Dickinson’s dashes and substitutions make the hymn-like pattern flexible.

Slant rhymes such as “me”/“Immortality” and “Day”/“Eternity” echo without fully closing the sound.

## Literary devices

### Personification

```
He kindly stopped for me—
```

Death becomes a courteous driver, allowing an abstract event to unfold as an ambiguous social encounter.

### Extended metaphor

```
The Carriage held but just Ourselves—
And Immortality.
```

The carriage sustains a model of dying as departure, passage, burial, and possible continuation.

### Reversal

```
Or rather—He passed Us—
```

The correction unsettles the apparent direction and exposes the speaker’s unstable perception of time and death.

## Historical context

Written around 1862, the poem was published in Poems by Emily Dickinson in 1890. Early editors titled it “The Chariot,” omitted the fourth stanza, and regularized wording.[2]

Cristanne Miller calls the omitted stanza an emotional turning point and reads the opening as an ironic portrait of Victorian gentility and repression.[2]

## What critics say

> “For many modern readers, the omitted fourth stanza is the emotional heart of the poem and its turning point.”
>
> — Cristanne Miller, [White Heat, Dartmouth College](https://journeys.dartmouth.edu/whiteheat/jan8-14f479/)

> “The poem becomes a satiric portrait of Victorian gentility and repression …”
>
> — Cristanne Miller, [White Heat, Dartmouth College](https://journeys.dartmouth.edu/whiteheat/jan8-14f479/)

## Common questions

### What is the meaning?

The poem imagines death as a carriage journey through life, burial, and an uncertain eternity.

### What does the house represent?

It is a grave described through domestic architecture.

### What meter does it use?

A flexible form of common meter with slant rhyme and distinctive dashes.

## References

- [Academy of American Poets](https://poets.org/poem/because-i-could-not-stop-death-479)

- [Cristanne Miller, White Heat, Dartmouth College](https://journeys.dartmouth.edu/whiteheat/jan8-14f479/)

- [Cristanne Miller, White Heat, Dartmouth College](https://journeys.dartmouth.edu/whiteheat/jan8-14f479/)

- [Project Gutenberg](https://www.gutenberg.org/files/12242/12242-h/12242-h.htm)

## Open the editor

Write with this poem’s meter in the editor: https://lyriic.com/write/common-meter

# Bless God, he went as soldiers analysis

Bless God, he went as soldiers — Emily Dickinson (1890)

This analysis follows the poem’s blend of military imagery, prayer, and conditional courage.

Full text from [Bless God, he went as soldiers](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Poems:_Third_Series/Bless_God,_he_went_as_soldiers). Public domain in the US (Written mid-nineteenth century and published posthumously in Poems, Third Series (1896), so the poem is public domain in the United States.).

## Summary

The speaker imagines a beloved man entering battle with a musket and asks God to place him among the bravest blessed.

```
BLESS God, he went as soldiers,
His musket on his breast;
Grant, God, he charge the bravest
```

Seeing him in heavenly white would let the speaker face an unnamed foe without fear.[4]

## Meaning and interpretation

Faith is desired but not fully possessed. The speaker’s courage depends on seeing visible proof that the beloved has reached a safe, honored afterlife.[2]

```
Please God, might I behold him
In epauletted white,
I should not fear the foe then
```

The subjunctive “might” keeps the requested vision unresolved, so the poem ends before certainty arrives.[2]

## Themes

### Faith and uncertainty

Bless, Grant, and Please make belief sound like a request awaiting an answer rather than a settled creed.[4]

### Courage through example

The beloved’s imagined bravery becomes the speaker’s possible source of courage.

### War and spiritual language

Musket, charge, foe, and fight overlap with God, blest, and white, so secular battle and spiritual trial share one vocabulary.[2]

## Form and meter

Two quatrains broadly resemble common meter, with flexible stresses and hymn-like short lines.[1]

Slant rhyme links “breast”/“blest,” while “white”/“fight” gives the second stanza a restrained closure.

## Literary devices

### Martial metaphor

```
His musket on his breast;
```

Spiritual status is described through enlistment, rank, and battle.

### Color imagery

```
In epauletted white
```

Military insignia and heavenly whiteness combine in one desired vision.

### Anaphora

```
BLESS God, he went as soldiers,
Grant, God, he charge the bravest
Please God, might I behold him
```

Repeated divine address creates a prayer-like rhythm.

## Historical context

Dickinson preserved the poem in an early fascicle around 1859; it appeared posthumously in Poems, Third Series in 1896.[3]

Scholar Shira Wolosky notes that Dickinson used martial vocabulary before the Civil War; this poem leaves its foe and fight deliberately unnamed.[2]

## What critics say

> “it is not clear whether or not the narrator can in the end obtain ‘victory.’”
>
> — Shira Wolosky, [Hitotsubashi University Repository](https://hit-u.repo.nii.ac.jp/record/2042924/files/jinbun0000900510.pdf)

> “Yet there is no resolution in the poem”
>
> — [BookishNerDan](https://slowlander.com/2019/06/07/page-45-of-864-of-emily-dickinsons-poems-as-she-preserved-them-2/)

## Common questions

### What is the meaning of “Bless God, he went as soldiers”?

The speaker wants a vision of a beloved soldier’s heavenly honor so she can face her own unnamed fight.

### What does “epauletted white” mean?

It joins decorated military clothing with heavenly white, imagining the beloved as both officer and blessed spirit.

### What is the poem’s form?

Two flexible, hymn-like quatrains that broadly resemble common meter, with slant rhyme.

## References

- [Wikisource](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Poems:_Third_Series/Bless_God,_he_went_as_soldiers)

- [Shira Wolosky, Hitotsubashi University Repository](https://hit-u.repo.nii.ac.jp/record/2042924/files/jinbun0000900510.pdf)

- [Morgan Library & Museum](https://www.themorgan.org/exhibitions/online/emily-dickinson/9)

- [BookishNerDan](https://slowlander.com/2019/06/07/page-45-of-864-of-emily-dickinsons-poems-as-she-preserved-them-2/)

## Open the editor

Write with this poem’s meter in the editor: https://lyriic.com/write/common-meter

# Chicago analysis

Chicago — Carl Sandburg (1914)

Sandburg admits Chicago’s violence and hunger before celebrating its labor, energy, and civic pride.

Full text from [Chicago](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poetrymagazine/poems/12840/chicago). Public domain in the US (First published in Poetry in 1914, before the US public-domain cutoff.).

## Summary

The speaker names Chicago through industrial occupations, concedes its vice and brutality, then answers its critics with an image of a laughing worker.

```
Hog Butcher for the World,
Tool Maker, Stacker of Wheat,
Player with Railroads and the Nation's Freight Handler;
```

The city’s greatness is grounded in work rather than polished respectability.

## Meaning and interpretation

The defense persuades because it does not pretend Chicago is innocent. Pride and social damage coexist in the same urban body.

```
Come and show me another city with lifted head singing so proud to be alive and coarse and strong and cunning.
```

The final laughter makes resilience a public, physical act.[2]

## Themes

### Industrial labor

The opening catalogue identifies Chicago through slaughtering, tools, grain, and freight.

### Clear-eyed civic pride

Crime and hunger are admitted before the speaker celebrates the city.

### Youth and resilience

```
Building, breaking, rebuilding,
Under the smoke, dust all over his mouth, laughing with white teeth,
```

Rebuilding turns hardship into continued motion.

## Form and meter

This is free verse with no fixed stanza, rhyme scheme, or regular meter. Its form comes from catalogues, punctuation, and changing line length.

Long sentences are interrupted by one-word action lines such as “Shoveling” and “Laughing!”, creating a physical rhythm.

## Literary devices

### Personification

```
here is a tall bold slugger set vivid against the little soft cities;
```

Chicago becomes a working fighter with sweat, teeth, ribs, and laughter.

### Catalogue

```
Bareheaded,
Shoveling,
Wrecking,
```

Accumulated occupations make civic identity collective.

### Repetition

```
Laughing!
Laughing the stormy, husky, brawling laughter of Youth,
```

Repeated laughter gathers force at the close.

## Historical context

Sandburg moved to Chicago in 1912 and worked as a reporter. The National Park Service connects his early writing with labor rights and unsafe working conditions.[2]

Harriet Monroe published the poem in Poetry in March 1914; it later appeared in Chicago Poems (1916).[3]

## What critics say

> “Sandburg’s early writings tackled social justice, human dignity, and labor rights.”
>
> — [National Park Service](https://www.nps.gov/articles/000/carl-sandburg-and-chicago.htm)

> “Chicago became one of the best known works of 20th century American literature.”
>
> — [Carl Sandburg Home National Historic Site](https://www.nps.gov/carl/learn/historyculture/chicago.htm)

## Common questions

### What is the meaning?

Chicago celebrates industrial strength and working people without denying crime, poverty, or corruption.

### Why Big Shoulders?

The phrase personifies the city as a strong laborer carrying collective work and burden.

### What form is used?

Free verse shaped by repetition, catalogues, and long and short lines.

## References

- [Poetry Foundation](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poetrymagazine/poems/12840/chicago)

- [National Park Service](https://www.nps.gov/articles/000/carl-sandburg-and-chicago.htm)

- [Carl Sandburg Home National Historic Site](https://www.nps.gov/carl/learn/historyculture/chicago.htm)

- [EBSCO Research Starters](https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/literature-and-writing/chicago-carl-sandburg)

## Open the editor

Read the poem in the zen editor: https://lyriic.com/write

# Doubt No More That Oberon analysis

Doubt No More That Oberon — Edna St. Vincent Millay (1921)

Millay uses myth and spring to argue that wonder can persist in a damaged age.

Full text from [Second April](https://monadnock.net/millay/). Public domain in the US (Published in Second April in 1921, before the US public-domain cutoff.).

## Summary

The speaker insists that Oberon and Pan should not be dismissed as childish inventions. Against a sorrowful present, ordinary spring becomes evidence of persistence.[1]

```
Doubt no more that Oberon—
Never doubt that Pan
Lived, and played a reed,
```

The dogwood and returning birds replace vanished fauns and fays as modest signs of wonder.

## Meaning and interpretation

Wonder survives not as perfect myth but as recurring natural life. The poem’s hope is limited: flowers bear no fruit and birds cannot sing, yet they return.

```
Still the dog-wood dares to raise—
Healthy tree, with trunk and root—
Ivory bowls that bear no fruit,
```

“Dare” makes seasonal growth a resistance to despair.[2]

## Themes

### Wonder versus despair

The imperative “Doubt no more” treats belief as an active answer to cynicism.

### Nature’s renewal

```
And the starlings and the jays—
Birds that cannot even sing—
Dare to come again in spring!
```

Imperfect return becomes proof of persistence.

### Beauty with mortality

Death is acknowledged directly before the poem turns to growth, so hope does not erase loss.

## Form and meter

A sixteen-line single-stanza lyric uses short, irregular lines and audible but varied rhyme.

Repeated verbs—“Lived” and “Dare”—supply structural unity more than a fixed meter does.

## Literary devices

### Mythological allusion

```
Never doubt that Pan
Lived, and played a reed, and ran
```

Oberon and Pan enlarge a spring scene into a debate about lost enchantment.

### Personification

```
Still the dog-wood dares to raise—
```

“Dares” makes growth sound like deliberate defiance.

### Understatement

```
Birds that cannot even sing—
```

Compromised beauty makes the poem’s hope demanding rather than sentimental.

## Historical context

The poem appeared in Second April (1921), a collection shaped by postwar and post-pandemic mortality; contemporary readers described its gloom as nearly outweighing its lyricism.[2]

Millay’s Pan belongs to a literary conversation about whether pagan nature figures could survive in modernity.

## What critics say

> “they breathed a gloom so unmitigated as almost to outweigh their lyrical quality.”
>
> — V. M. Braganza, [Los Angeles Review of Books](https://lareviewofbooks.org/blog/essays/second-april/)

> “Pan was an insider and not an outsider”
>
> — Thomas Burnett Swann, [WSFA Journal](https://fanac.org/fanzines/WSFA_Journal/WSFA_Journal68.pdf)

## Common questions

### What is the meaning?

The poem argues that wonder and renewal remain possible even in a sorrowful age.

### What are its themes?

Wonder, despair, natural renewal, and beauty alongside mortality.

### What form does it use?

A sixteen-line single-stanza lyric with irregular rhythm and recurring rhyme.

## References

- [Monadnock Valley Press](https://monadnock.net/millay/)

- [V. M. Braganza, Los Angeles Review of Books](https://lareviewofbooks.org/blog/essays/second-april/)

- [Thomas Burnett Swann, WSFA Journal](https://fanac.org/fanzines/WSFA_Journal/WSFA_Journal68.pdf)

- [Literary Ladies Guide](https://www.literaryladiesguide.com/classic-women-authors-poetry/second-april-by-edna-st-vincent-millay-1921-full-text/)

## Open the editor

Write with this poem’s open form in the editor: https://lyriic.com/write

# Dreams analysis

Dreams — Langston Hughes (1922)

Hughes presents dreams as necessary for life’s movement, purpose, and possibility.

Full text from [Dreams](https://poets.org/poem/dreams). Public domain in the US (Documented as a 1922 work, before the US public-domain cutoff.).

## Summary

The speaker commands readers to hold fast to dreams. Without them, life is first injured and unable to fly, then barren and frozen.

```
Hold fast to dreams
For if dreams die
Life is a broken-winged bird
```

The second stanza intensifies the warning by replacing impaired movement with sterility.

## Meaning and interpretation

Dreams can mean hopes, aspirations, or communal possibility. Hughes does not treat them as decoration; they sustain movement and growth.

```
For when dreams go
Life is a barren field
Frozen with snow.
```

The shift from “if” to “when” makes loss feel both avoidable and inevitable.[2]

## Themes

### Hope and aspiration

The repeated imperative makes hope an active practice rather than passive wishing.

### Loss and sterility

```
Life is a broken-winged bird
That cannot fly.
```

The injured bird turns dreamlessness into lost freedom.

### Possibility

The barren field shows that without dreams, growth and future action become impossible.

## Form and meter

Two compact quatrains repeat the opening command. Short, varied lines create plainspoken urgency.

ABCB-like echoes, especially “die”/“fly,” provide musical cohesion without elaborate rhyme.

## Literary devices

### Metaphor

```
Life is a broken-winged bird
That cannot fly.
```

An abstract loss becomes physical incapacity.

### Extended imagery

```
Life is a barren field
Frozen with snow.
```

Barren ground and cold suggest sterility and stillness.

### Repetition

```
Hold fast to dreams
...
Hold fast to dreams
```

The refrain keeps the central instruction foregrounded.

## Historical context

The poem is commonly dated 1922; related publication evidence places it in The World Tomorrow in 1923.[3]

Hughes’s place in the Harlem Renaissance makes the preservation of dreams legible both as individual aspiration and collective hope.[2]

## What critics say

> “The speaker compares life after the loss of dreams to “a broken-winged bird / That cannot fly” and “a barren field / Frozen with snow.””
>
> — [LitCharts](https://www.litcharts.com/poetry/langston-hughes/dreams)

> “‘Dreams’ by Langston Hughes is a short poem of 8 lines”
>
> — [Study.com](https://study.com/academy/lesson/dreams-by-langston-hughes-summary-analysis.html)

## Common questions

### What is the meaning?

Dreams sustain purpose, movement, hope, and the possibility of growth.

### What are the themes?

Hope, aspiration, loss, freedom, and emotional barrenness.

### What is the form?

Two quatrains with short lines, repetition, and loose ABCB echoes.

## References

- [Academy of American Poets](https://poets.org/poem/dreams)

- [LitCharts](https://www.litcharts.com/poetry/langston-hughes/dreams)

- [Study.com](https://study.com/academy/lesson/dreams-by-langston-hughes-summary-analysis.html)

- [Poem Analysis](https://poemanalysis.com/langston-hughes/dreams/)

## Open the editor

Write with this poem’s rhythm in the editor: https://lyriic.com/write

# Each and All analysis

Each and All — Ralph Waldo Emerson (1839)

Emerson shows that beauty and meaning depend on the living whole surrounding each object.

Full text from [Each and All](https://poets.org/poem/each-and-all). Public domain in the US (First published in 1839, before the US public-domain cutoff.).

## Summary

A sparrow, shells, and a lover’s bride lose their beauty when removed from the contexts that made them meaningful.[1]

```
All are needed by each one;
Nothing is fair or good alone.
```

The speaker finally returns to the whole natural scene and yields to it.

## Meaning and interpretation

Beauty is relational rather than portable: the river, sky, sun, sand, and sea cannot be carried home with their objects.

```
For I did not bring home the river and sky;
He sang to my ear,—they sang to my eye.
```

Possession gives way to participation.[2]

## Themes

### Organic unity

Each object participates in a larger system of natural and social meanings.

### Beauty and context

```
Had left their beauty on the shore,
With the sun, and the sand, and the wild uproar.
```

Beauty includes place, sound, light, and motion.

### Possession versus participation

The speaker’s attempts to bring things home isolate what he admired; the ending reverses that movement.

## Form and meter

The 51-line poem unfolds as a continuous argument through linked examples, using flexible songlike rhythm.

Paired end rhymes and conversational pauses give the long narrative a measured movement.

## Literary devices

### Aphorism

```
All are needed by each one;
Nothing is fair or good alone.
```

Balanced syntax turns the governing idea into a memorable principle.

### Sensory imagery

```
The bubbles of the latest wave
Fresh pearls to their enamel gave;
```

The shore’s beauty is environmental, not merely visual.

### Simile

```
Like the bird from the woodlands to the cage;—
```

The romantic example echoes the earlier caged sparrow.

## Historical context

The poem was published in the Western Messenger in 1839 and reflects Emerson’s Transcendentalist interest in nature and unity.[2]

Its local field, shore, and woodland scenes expand into a philosophy of interdependence.

## What critics say

> “The theme of ‘organic unity’.”
>
> — [Türk Dilbilim](https://turkdilbilim.wordpress.com/2020/10/11/each-and-all-by-emerson-an-analysis/)

> “Beauty comes from the connection of all living and non-living things”
>
> — [Poem Analysis](https://poemanalysis.com/ralph-waldo-emerson/each-and-all/)

## Common questions

### What is the meaning?

Meaning and beauty depend on relationships among objects, places, and people.

### What are the themes?

Organic unity, beauty in context, perception, and possession.

### What is the form?

A continuous 51-line poem with flexible rhythm and paired rhyme.

## References

- [Academy of American Poets](https://poets.org/poem/each-and-all)

- [Türk Dilbilim](https://turkdilbilim.wordpress.com/2020/10/11/each-and-all-by-emerson-an-analysis/)

- [Poem Analysis](https://poemanalysis.com/ralph-waldo-emerson/each-and-all/)

- [EBSCO Research Starters](https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/history/poetry-emerson-ralph-waldo-emerson)

## Open the editor

Write with this poem’s open form in the editor: https://lyriic.com/write

# Fire and Ice analysis

Fire and Ice — Robert Frost (1920)

Frost turns an end-of-the-world question into a study of destructive human feeling.

Full text from [Fire and Ice](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poems/44263/fire-and-ice). Public domain in the US (First printed in 1920, before the US public-domain cutoff.).

## Summary

The speaker weighs fire and ice as possible ends of the world, linking fire with desire and ice with hate.

```
Some say the world will end in fire,
Some say in ice.
From what I’ve tasted of desire
```

Both forces prove sufficient for destruction.

## Meaning and interpretation

Fire suggests consuming appetite; ice suggests hatred that hardens and separates. The conversational tone makes catastrophe sound casually plausible.

```
For destruction ice
Is also great
And would suffice.
```

“Suffice” is understated and chilling: global ruin is treated as a question of adequacy.[2]

## Themes

### Desire

Personal experience makes fire an embodied metaphor for appetite and excess.

### Hate

Ice gives emotional coldness a destructive physical form.

### Human self-destruction

```
I think I know enough of hate
To say that for destruction ice
```

The cosmic question becomes a moral inventory of human feeling.

## Form and meter

The nine-line single stanza is mostly iambic tetrameter, with shorter lines that compress the close.

ABA ABC BCB interlocks the fire, ice, and hate rhyme families; the form keeps the alternatives balanced.

## Literary devices

### Allegory

```
Some say the world will end in fire,
Some say in ice.
```

Elements become figures for desire and hate.

### Antithesis

Repeated “Some say” establishes a debate that ends in equivalence.

### Understatement

```
And would suffice.
```

A mild verb carries the scale of annihilation.

## Historical context

Frost’s poem was printed in Harper’s Magazine in December 1920 and collected in 1923, after the First World War made mass destruction newly immediate.[4]

Readers often connect its interlocking rhyme with terza rima, though that Dantean association remains an interpretive lens.

## What critics say

> “Though the speaker presents two choices, they both amount to the same thing: the end of the world”
>
> — [LitCharts](https://www.litcharts.com/poetry/robert-frost/fire-and-ice)

> “fire gets more verbal space, but ice gets the last word.”
>
> — [Poetry Lovers’ Page](https://www.poetryloverspage.com/poets/frost/fire_and_ice/literary-analysis)

## Common questions

### What is the meaning?

Desire and hate are different but equally sufficient forces of destruction.

### What do fire and ice symbolize?

Fire symbolizes desire; ice symbolizes hate or emotional coldness.

### What is the form?

A nine-line stanza with interlocking rhyme and mostly iambic tetrameter.

## References

- [Poetry Foundation](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poems/44263/fire-and-ice)

- [LitCharts](https://www.litcharts.com/poetry/robert-frost/fire-and-ice)

- [Poetry Lovers’ Page](https://www.poetryloverspage.com/poets/frost/fire_and_ice/literary-analysis)

- [Interesting Literature](https://interestingliterature.com/2019/12/analysis-robert-frost-fire-and-ice/)

## Open the editor

Write with this poem’s meter in the editor: https://lyriic.com/write/iambic-tetrameter

---

# First Fig analysis

First Fig — Edna St. Vincent Millay (1920)

Millay’s candle metaphor makes a brief, intense life both risky and beautiful.

Full text from [First Fig](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poetrymagazine/poems/14095/first-fig). Public domain in the US (Published in 1920, before the US public-domain cutoff.).

## Summary

The speaker’s candle burns at both ends, promising a short night but producing a lovely light.[1]

```
My candle burns at both ends;
It will not last the night;
```

Friends and foes are invited to witness the speaker’s intense choice.

## Meaning and interpretation

The candle represents a life spent with unusual energy, appetite, or creative and erotic freedom. The exact behavior remains deliberately open.

```
But ah, my foes, and oh, my friends—
It gives a lovely light!
```

The final exclamation turns a warning about exhaustion into celebration.[2]

## Themes

### Intensity and transience

Brilliance is inseparable from self-consumption and limited time.

### Defiance

Addressing foes and friends together places public judgment beneath personal choice.

### Present beauty

```
It gives a lovely light!
```

The poem values immediate experience over future duration.

## Form and meter

The four-line lyric uses a common-meter or ballad-stanza pattern with alternating longer and shorter lines.

ABAB rhyme makes the rebellious declaration polished, memorable, and songlike.

## Literary devices

### Extended metaphor

```
My candle burns at both ends;
```

The flame joins pleasure to risk and brightness to self-consumption.

### Apostrophe

```
my foes, and oh, my friends—
```

The public address makes the speaker’s choice performative and witnessed.

### Alliteration

The repeated b sounds give the opening momentum; “lovely light” softens the final image.

## Historical context

The poem appeared in Poetry in 1918 and opened A Few Figs from Thistles in 1920. Scholarship reads the volume as challenging gendered expectations about time, work, and sexuality.[2]

Its familiar meter gives a modern, defiant claim a traditional lyric frame.

## What critics say

> “the poems in this short series debunk a conservative economy of time and work”
>
> — [Textual Cultures](https://scholarworks.iu.edu/journals/index.php/textual/article/download/2117/26571/45516)

> “It gives a lovely light!”
>
> — [Women Writers](https://pressbooks.marshall.edu/womenwriters/chapter/edna-st-vincent-millay/)

## Common questions

### What is the meaning?

The poem celebrates living intensely despite the cost of a shorter, less restrained life.

### What does the candle symbolize?

It symbolizes life, creative energy, and possibly erotic freedom.

### What is the form?

A four-line common-meter quatrain with ABAB rhyme.

## References

- [Poetry Foundation](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poetrymagazine/poems/14095/first-fig)

- [Textual Cultures](https://scholarworks.iu.edu/journals/index.php/textual/article/download/2117/26571/45516)

- [Women Writers](https://pressbooks.marshall.edu/womenwriters/chapter/edna-st-vincent-millay/)

- [LitCharts](https://www.litcharts.com/poetry/edna-st-vincent-millay/first-fig)

## Open the editor

Write with this poem’s meter in the editor: https://lyriic.com/write/common-meter

# Fog analysis

Fog — Carl Sandburg (1916)

Sandburg makes a passing weather event mysterious by giving it the silent movements of a cat.

Full text from [Fog](https://poets.org/poem/fog). Public domain in the US (First published in Chicago Poems in 1916, before the US public-domain cutoff.).

## Summary

Fog arrives quietly, settles over harbor and city, watches, and then leaves.

```
The fog comes
on little cat feet.
```

The extended metaphor gives ordinary weather the presence of a self-possessed animal.

## Meaning and interpretation

The cat image lets readers sense stealth, patience, and agency without a narrative explanation.

```
It sits looking
over harbor and city
on silent haunches
```

The final movement keeps the poem open: fog visits, alters perception, and disappears.[2]

## Themes

### Nature’s mystery

A familiar phenomenon becomes alert, independent, and slightly unknowable.

### Transience

```
and then moves on.
```

The poem’s six lines mirror fog’s brief appearance.

### Nature and city

Fog moves over both harbor and city, placing an organic force above an organized landscape.

## Form and meter

The poem is free verse in six lines, arranged as a two-line couplet followed by four lines.

Its quiet rhythm comes from varied line lengths and plain syntax; the compact image resembles an American haiku without being a traditional Japanese haiku.

## Literary devices

### Extended metaphor

```
The fog comes
on little cat feet.
```

Feet, haunches, and movement sustain the cat comparison.

### Personification

```
It sits looking
over harbor and city
```

Fog receives an animal’s posture and attention.

### Enjambment

```
It sits looking
over harbor and city
```

The break delays the object of looking and extends the imagined gaze.

## Historical context

The poem appeared in Sandburg’s 1916 collection Chicago Poems. It is associated with his attempt to make a brief, image-centered American haiku.[3]

Although Chicago is plausible, the text says only “harbor and city,” leaving the setting open.

## What critics say

> “The comparison makes the fog ... seem mysterious and unknowable.”
>
> — [LitCharts](https://www.litcharts.com/poetry/carl-sandburg/fog)

> “the loveliness of ... a fog coming on ‘little cat feet,’”
>
> — Harriet Monroe, [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fog_(poem))

## Common questions

### What is the meaning?

Fog is a quiet, catlike visitor whose brief presence reveals nature’s mystery and beauty.

### Why a cat?

Cats move silently, watch from stillness, and appear and disappear independently.

### What form is used?

Six lines of free verse in two stanzas, with an image-centered, haiku-like compression.

## References

- [Academy of American Poets](https://poets.org/poem/fog)

- [LitCharts](https://www.litcharts.com/poetry/carl-sandburg/fog)

- [Harriet Monroe, Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fog_(poem))

- [Poem Analysis](https://poemanalysis.com/carl-sandburg/fog/)

## Open the editor

Write with this poem’s open form in the editor: https://lyriic.com/write

# Go and Catch a Falling Star analysis

Song: Go and catch a falling star — John Donne (1633)

This analysis explains how Donne turns supernatural commands and a brisk song form into a bitter argument about fidelity.

Full text from [Song — full poem](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Song:_Go_and_catch_a_falling_star). Public domain in the US (First published in Donne's collected poems in 1633, well before the US public-domain cutoff.).

## Summary

The speaker orders a listener to perform impossible tasks, then asks him to search for a woman who is both true and fair.[2]

```
GO and catch a falling star,
Get with child a mandrake root,
Tell me where all past years are,
```

The final stanza withdraws the apparent invitation: even if such a woman were found, she would be false before the speaker arrived.[3]

## Meaning and interpretation

Donne makes fidelity seem less attainable than catching a star or hearing mermaids. The comic quest turns a conventional complaint about infidelity into a memorable paradox.[2]

```
And swear
No where
Lives a woman true and fair.
```

The speaker’s misogynistic generalization is a historical literary posture, not a neutral account of relationships; the song’s musical confidence makes it sound persuasive.[2]

## Themes

### Fidelity and skepticism

The search for a faithful woman becomes an impossible quest, and the ending turns skepticism into a universal judgment.[2]

### Gender and power

The poem treats women’s supposed inconstancy as a conventionally gendered claim that modern readers can examine critically.[2]

### Wonder and disillusionment

Stars, mandrakes, mermaids, and a ten-thousand-day journey create marvels against which human constancy is judged.

## Form and meter

The poem has three nine-line stanzas. Each uses ABABCC followed by a rhyming triplet, giving the argument brisk song-like momentum.[3]

Its predominant rhythm is trochaic tetrameter; the short “And find / What wind” lines sharpen each stanza’s punchline.[3]

## Literary devices

### Hyperbole

```
Ride ten thousand days and nights
Till Age snow white hairs on thee;
```

The enormous journey makes fidelity sound beyond ordinary human effort.

### Imperative

```
GO and catch a falling star
```

The direct command gives the poem the energy of spoken banter.

### Folkloric allusion

```
Teach me to hear mermaids singing,
Or to keep off envy's stinging,
```

Supernatural references build a catalogue of strange possibilities.

### Irony

```
Such a pilgrimage were sweet.
Yet do not; I would not go,
```

The reversal exposes the gap between stated desire and settled disappointment.

## Historical context

The poem was first published posthumously in 1633 in the first collected edition of Donne’s poems. Its early-modern song form supports a witty complaint about inconstancy.[3]

The speaker’s claim belongs to a gendered literary convention and can be read both as clever rhetoric and as prejudice.[2]

## What critics say

> “The poem's rhyme scheme, relatively steady meter, and clear hyperbole make its tone feel light-hearted and satirical, but the speaker also seems to harbor genuine melancholy, bitterness, and cynicism towards women and relationships.”
>
> — [LitCharts](https://www.litcharts.com/poetry/john-donne/song-go-and-catch-a-falling-star)

> “John Donne enforced a tight structure on his song Go and Catch a Falling Star”
>
> — [Literary Theory and Criticism](https://literariness.org/2020/07/08/analysis-of-john-donnes-go-and-catch-a-falling-star/)

## Common questions

### What is the poem’s main meaning?

The speaker claims that a beautiful, faithful woman is as impossible to find as a supernatural wonder, though the claim is deliberately witty and gendered.

### What are its main themes?

Fidelity, skepticism, wonder, gender, and disillusionment shape the poem’s argument.

### What form does it use?

It has three nine-line stanzas with ABABCC and a closing triplet, in a brisk, predominantly trochaic song rhythm.

## References

- [Wikisource](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Song:_Go_and_catch_a_falling_star)

- [LitCharts](https://www.litcharts.com/poetry/john-donne/song-go-and-catch-a-falling-star)

- [Literary Theory and Criticism](https://literariness.org/2020/07/08/analysis-of-john-donnes-go-and-catch-a-falling-star/)

- [Poem Analysis](https://poemanalysis.com/john-donne/song-go-and-catch-a-falling-star/)

## Open the editor

Write with this poem’s meter in the editor: https://lyriic.com/write/trochaic-tetrameter

# Goblin Feet analysis

Goblin Feet — J. R. R. Tolkien (1915)

This analysis reads Tolkien’s poem as a spell-like journey from sensory enchantment to loss.

Full text from [Goblin Feet — full poem](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Goblin_Feet). Public domain in the US (First published in Oxford Poetry 1915, before the US public-domain cutoff.).

## Summary

The speaker follows a procession of tiny supernatural beings through a moonlit landscape of lanterns, wings, jewels, and padded feet.[2]

```
I am off down the road
Where the fairy lanterns glowed
And the little pretty flitter-mice are flying:
```

The procession fades around a turn, so delight becomes sorrow when the magic disappears.[2]

## Meaning and interpretation

The poem makes enchantment sensory: the reader hears humming, horns, robes, and feet while seeing lamps, colours, jewels, and wings.[2]

```
They are fading round the turn
Where the glow worms palely burn
And the echo of their padding feet is dying!
```

Wonder is temporary. The speaker wants to follow into another world, but the final line admits that magic’s disappearance is part of its emotional power.[2]

## Themes

### Wonder

Repeated lights, wings, and diminutive creatures make the fairy world feel close enough to enter.

### Transience and loss

Fading figures and dying echoes turn enchantment into an experience of grief.

### Desire for another world

Commands such as “Let me go!” turn observation into pursuit and longing.

## Form and meter

The four stanzas alternate longer descriptive passages with short exclamatory choruses. Flexible accentual-syllabic rhythm makes the poem songlike rather than strictly metrical.

Rhyme, internal sound, repeated “O!”, and recurring words such as “little” and “feet” create an incantatory pulse.[2]

## Literary devices

### Onomatopoeia

```
That warn you with their whirring and their humming.
```

Sound-imitating words make the invisible fairy traffic audible.

### Sensory imagery

```
O! the warmth! O! the hum!
O! the colours in the dark!
```

Accumulated sensations define the fairies more vividly than explanation.

### Repetition

```
O! the echo of their feet—of their happy little feet:
```

Repetition establishes a childlike, spell-like voice.

## Historical context

Tolkien wrote the poem on April 27–28, 1915, to please Edith Bratt, and Oxford Poetry 1915 published it in December.[3]

The Tolkien Library describes its fairy world as close to the Victorian depiction of fairies; Tolkien later regretted the poem’s diminutive tradition.[2]

## What critics say

> “The result was as close to the Victorian depiction of fairies as it can get.”
>
> — [Tolkien Library](https://tolkienlibrary.com/press/oxfordpoetry1915.php)

> “It celebrates the diminutive type of elf that Tolkien soon came to dislike”
>
> — [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goblin_Feet)

## Common questions

### What is Goblin Feet about?

It depicts a speaker following a fairy procession whose beauty and music fade into sorrow.

### What are its themes?

Wonder, sensory imagination, transience, loss, and the desire to cross into another world.

### What form does it use?

Its flexible, songlike rhythm alternates longer descriptions with exclamatory choruses.

## References

- [Wikisource](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Goblin_Feet)

- [Tolkien Library](https://tolkienlibrary.com/press/oxfordpoetry1915.php)

- [Tolkien Library](https://tolkienlibrary.com/booksedited/oxfordp/description.php)

- [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goblin_Feet)

## Open the editor

Write with this poem’s rhythm in the editor: https://lyriic.com/write

# Goliath and David analysis

Goliath and David — Robert Graves (1916)

Graves turns the biblical victory into a grim First World War parable; this analysis follows its reversal and war imagery.

Full text from [The Muse in Arms — full poem](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/The_Muse_in_Arms/In_Memoriam). Public domain in the US (First published in 1916, before the US public-domain cutoff.).

## Summary

Graves retells David and Goliath but announces that the familiar historian “Had not the heart to tell it right.”[2]

```
But the historian of that fight
Had not the heart to tell it right.
```

David’s sling and staff fail against shield and steel; Goliath survives and stands over the dead boy.[1]

## Meaning and interpretation

The reversal challenges the comforting underdog myth: courage cannot cancel superior material force in modern combat.[2]

```
(God's eyes are dim, His ears are shut.)
One cruel backhand sabre-cut—
```

The parenthesis makes the failure theological as well as military, while the dedication turns the rewritten legend into a memorial.[3]

## Themes

### Failure of heroic myth

The expected miracle is replaced by a blunt account of defeat.

### Unequal power

Pebble and wood are opposed to shield, armor, and steel.[2]

### Faith and divine silence

David trusts that God will save him, but the poem depicts no intervention.

### Grief and remembrance

The dedication identifies the poem with David Cuthbert Thomas, killed at Fricourt in March 1916.[3]

## Form and meter

The poem has a twelve-line opening stanza and a thirty-four-line battle stanza, mostly organized in rhyming couplets.[2]

The brisk couplets accommodate narrative action, while interruptions such as “Then ... but” fracture the traditional tale at the moment of reversal.

## Literary devices

### Biblical inversion

```
ONCE an earlier David took
Smooth pebbles from the brook:
```

The reversed title and altered outcome keep the biblical story present while denying its familiar moral.

### Onomatopoeia

```
Goliath's shield parries each cast.
Clang! clang! and clang! was David's last.
```

Metallic repetition makes the failed attack audible.

### Simile

```
The pebble, humming from the sling
Like a wild bee, flies a sure line
```

The lively simile emphasizes the pebble’s smallness against the giant’s equipment.

## Historical context

The poem is dedicated “For D. C. T., killed at Fricourt, March 1916”; the GMU notes identify David Cuthbert Thomas as Graves’s friend and fellow Royal Welch Fusilier.[3]

The spike-helmeted giant brings the biblical encounter into the First World War and its German military imagery.[1]

## What critics say

> “Graves has chosen to format this piece with a rhyme scheme of aabbccdd”
>
> — [Poem Analysis](https://poemanalysis.com/robert-graves/goliath-and-david/)

> “Like Wilfred Owen’s ‘Parable of the Old Man and the Young’ (1918), it generalizes the death of Thomas to illustrate a larger truth”
>
> — [Robert Graves Review](https://robertgravesreview.org/essay/378)

## Common questions

### What is the poem’s meaning?

It reverses the biblical victory to show how courage and faith can fail against overwhelming force.

### What are its themes?

Heroic myth, unequal power, divine silence, war, grief, and remembrance.

### What form does it use?

A two-stanza narrative built mainly from rhyming couplets, with varied meter and abrupt sound effects.

## References

- [Wikisource](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/The_Muse_in_Arms/In_Memoriam)

- [Poem Analysis](https://poemanalysis.com/robert-graves/goliath-and-david/)

- [George Mason University](https://mason.gmu.edu/~rnanian/Graves-GoliathandDavid.html)

- [Robert Graves Review](https://robertgravesreview.org/essay/378)

## Open the editor

Write with this poem’s rhythm in the editor: https://lyriic.com/write

# He Wishes for the Cloths of Heaven analysis

He Wishes for the Cloths of Heaven — W. B. Yeats (1899)

This analysis explains how Yeats turns heavenly fabric into a fragile offering of dreams.

Full text from [He wishes for the Cloths of Heaven](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/He_wishes_for_the_Cloths_of_Heaven). Public domain in the US (First published in The Wind Among the Reeds in 1899, before the US public-domain cutoff.).

## Summary

The speaker imagines giving a beloved the sky as embroidered cloth, then admits that poverty leaves only dreams to offer.[2]

```
Had I the heavens' embroidered cloths,
Enwrought with golden and silver light,
The blue and the dim and the dark cloths
```

The repeated image of spreading something beneath the beloved’s feet becomes a plea for emotional care.[2]

## Meaning and interpretation

Dreams are less tangible than wealth but more personal than any material gift. The speaker offers the inner life that produced the vision.[2]

```
But I, being poor, have only my dreams;
I have spread my dreams under your feet;
Tread softly because you tread on my dreams.
```

The final imperative makes love vulnerable: accepting the gift gives the beloved power to hurt the speaker.[2]

## Themes

### Love and vulnerability

The closing plea asks the beloved to handle the speaker’s exposed dreams gently.

### Imagination and poverty

Material lack redirects the gift toward imagination and feeling.

### Idealization

The beloved is placed above cloths made from the heavens, giving devotion a near-sacred scale.

## Form and meter

The poem is a single eight-line stanza divided into two quatrains by its ABAB CDCD rhyme pattern.[3]

Loose four-beat accentual verse and repeated end words make the short poem feel tightly woven rather than mechanically regular.[3]

## Literary devices

### Extended metaphor

```
Had I the heavens' embroidered cloths
```

The sky becomes fabric that can be embroidered and spread beneath the beloved.

### Visual imagery

```
The blue and the dim and the dark cloths
Of night and light and the half-light,
```

Gradations of light create a whole imagined sky.

### Repetition

```
I would spread the cloths under your feet:
But I, being poor, have only my dreams;
```

The shift from hypothetical cloths to actual dreams changes fantasy into an offering.

## Historical context

Yeats published the poem in The Wind Among the Reeds in 1899; the earlier title was “Aedh Wishes for the Cloths of Heaven.”[3]

The Academy of American Poets records Joseph Hone’s remark that this poem was “the way to lose” a lady, a comment that underscores its vulnerable rather than triumphant courtship.[4]

## What critics say

> “Love, this short but powerful poem suggests, can feel at once transcendently beautiful and perilous.”
>
> — [LitCharts](https://www.litcharts.com/poetry/william-butler-yeats/he-wishes-for-the-cloths-of-heaven)

> “Aedh wishes for the Cloths of Heaven is the way to lose one.”
>
> — [Academy of American Poets](https://poets.org/poem/aedh-wishes-cloths-heaven)

## Common questions

### What is the poem’s meaning?

The speaker offers dreams instead of the heavenly riches he imagines and asks the beloved to treat them gently.

### What are its themes?

Love, vulnerability, imagination, poverty, and idealization.

### What form does it use?

One eight-line stanza with an ABAB CDCD rhyme pattern and loose four-beat rhythm.

## References

- [Wikisource](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/He_wishes_for_the_Cloths_of_Heaven)

- [LitCharts](https://www.litcharts.com/poetry/william-butler-yeats/he-wishes-for-the-cloths-of-heaven)

- [LitCharts](https://www.litcharts.com/poetry/william-butler-yeats/he-wishes-for-the-cloths-of-heaven)

- [Academy of American Poets](https://poets.org/poem/aedh-wishes-cloths-heaven)

## Open the editor

Write with this poem’s rhythm in the editor: https://lyriic.com/write

# Hope Is the Thing with Feathers analysis

Hope Is the Thing with Feathers — Emily Dickinson (1891)

This analysis explains how Dickinson turns hope into a wordless bird that sings through hardship.

Full text from [Hope is the thing with feathers](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poems/42889/hope-is-the-thing-with-feathers-314). Public domain in the US (First published posthumously in 1891, before the US public-domain cutoff.).

## Summary

Dickinson imagines hope as a bird living in the soul, singing continuously and offering warmth without demanding payment.[2]

```
“Hope” is the thing with feathers -
That perches in the soul -
And sings the tune without the words -
```

The bird’s song survives gale, cold, and sea; the final stanza says it has never asked even a crumb in return.[1]

## Meaning and interpretation

The central metaphor makes hope intimate yet independent: it lives within the soul but does not depend on words or conscious effort.[2]

```
And sweetest - in the Gale - is heard -
And sore must be the storm -
That could abash the little Bird
```

Hope is strongest under pressure and radically selfless, sustaining people without demanding certainty or proof.[2]

## Themes

### Inner resource

The bird perches in the soul, presenting hope as a capacity already present within a person.

### Endurance

Gale, storm, chill, and sea test the bird’s persistence.

### Generosity

Hope keeps people warm but asks no crumb in return.

## Form and meter

Three quatrains broadly follow common meter, alternating iambic tetrameter and trimeter.[3]

Dashes interrupt the hymn-like pulse, while slant rhymes keep the form flexible rather than mechanically neat.[2]

## Literary devices

### Extended metaphor

```
“Hope” is the thing with feathers -
```

Perching, singing, and surviving weather develop the bird comparison across the poem.

### Personification

```
It asked a crumb - of me.
```

Hope is given intention, then shown to ask for nothing.

### Sound imagery

```
And sings the tune without the words -
```

The wordless song suggests that hope can be felt before it is explained.

## Historical context

Dickinson wrote the poem around 1861; it was first published posthumously in 1891.[4]

Susannah Fullerton describes it as hymn-like and emphasizes Dickinson’s dashes, capitalization, and the bird’s persistence through storms.[2]

## What critics say

> “This poem is like a hymn. In its use of the bird as an extended metaphor, Hope does not disappear when it faces storms of hardship, but sings on.”
>
> — [Susannah Fullerton](https://susannahfullerton.com.au/emily-dickinson-hope-is-the-thing-with-feathers/)

> “Hope is the thing with feathers is a kind of hymn of praise”
>
> — [LitCharts](https://www.litcharts.com/poetry/emily-dickinson/hope-is-the-thing-with-feathers)

## Common questions

### What is the poem’s meaning?

Hope is a persistent inner strength that sings through hardship and gives without asking anything in return.

### What does the bird symbolize?

It symbolizes hope as a living, resilient, selfless force within the soul.

### What meter does the poem use?

It broadly uses common meter, with Dickinson’s dashes and slant rhymes disrupting a strict hymn pattern.

## References

- [Poetry Foundation](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poems/42889/hope-is-the-thing-with-feathers-314)

- [Susannah Fullerton](https://susannahfullerton.com.au/emily-dickinson-hope-is-the-thing-with-feathers/)

- [LitCharts](https://www.litcharts.com/poetry/emily-dickinson/hope-is-the-thing-with-feathers)

- [Owl Eyes](https://www.owleyes.org/text/hope-is-the-thing-with-feathers)

## Open the editor

Write with this poem’s meter in the editor: https://lyriic.com/write/common-meter
