# Paradise Lost analysis

Paradise Lost — John Milton (1667)

This Paradise Lost analysis explains its meaning, themes, form, and major literary devices.

Full text from [Full text of Paradise Lost](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Paradise_Lost_(1667)/Book_I). Public domain in the US (First published in 1667, before 1931; the original work is public domain in the United States.).

## Summary

The Book I invocation names humanity’s first disobedience, the loss of Eden, and the epic’s aim to explain divine providence. Milton calls on a Christian muse rather than a classical one.[1]

```
Of Mans First Disobedience, and the Fruit
Of that Forbidden Tree, whose mortal tast
Brought Death into the World, and all our woe,
```

## Meaning and interpretation

The opening combines epic ambition with dependence: the poet intends a song that will exceed classical precedent but asks the Spirit to illuminate what is dark in him.[2]

```
That to the highth of this great Argument
I may assert Eternal Providence,
And justifie the wayes of God to men.
```

## Themes

### Meaning and interpretation

The opening combines epic ambition with dependence: the poet intends a song that will exceed classical precedent but asks the Spirit to illuminate what is dark in him.[1]

### Form and language

Paradise Lost is English heroic blank verse: unrhymed iambic pentameter varied by enjambment, pauses, and inversions.[2]

## Form and meter

Paradise Lost is English heroic blank verse: unrhymed iambic pentameter varied by enjambment, pauses, and inversions.[2]

```
Of Mans First Disobedience, and the Fruit
Of that Forbidden Tree, whose mortal tast
Brought Death into the World, and all our woe,
```

## Literary devices

### Imagery and contrast

```
Of Mans First Disobedience, and the Fruit
Of that Forbidden Tree, whose mortal tast
Brought Death into the World, and all our woe,
```

Concrete images turn the poem’s central abstraction into a memorable scene.

### Repetition and sound

```
That to the highth of this great Argument
I may assert Eternal Providence,
And justifie the wayes of God to men.
```

Repetition and patterned sound give the argument emotional force and shape the reader’s pace.

## Historical context

The work belongs to the public-domain period identified by its first publication year. Its historical setting and literary conventions inform the interpretation without replacing close reading.[1]

Paradise Lost is English heroic blank verse: unrhymed iambic pentameter varied by enjambment, pauses, and inversions.[2]

## What critics say

> “Milton’s invocation is extremely humble, expressing his utter dependence on God’s grace in speaking through him.”
>
> — SparkNotes editors, [SparkNotes](https://www.sparknotes.com/poetry/paradiselost/section1/)

> “Of Mans First Disobedience, and the Fruit”
>
> — John Milton, [Wikisource](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Paradise_Lost_(1667)/Book_I)

## Common questions

### What is the main meaning of Paradise Lost?

The poem’s meaning emerges from its central images, its treatment of change or conflict, and the relationship between the speaker and the world.

### What are the main themes in Paradise Lost?

Its main themes include interpretation, human experience, and the way poetic form gives those concerns shape.

### What form does Paradise Lost use?

The poem’s form is described in the analysis above; meter, lineation, repetition, and sound all contribute to its effect.

# Pastoral analysis

Pastoral — William Carlos Williams (1917)

This Pastoral analysis explains its meaning, themes, form, and major literary devices.

Full text from [Full text of Pastoral](https://www.gutenberg.org/files/51997/51997-0.txt). Public domain in the US (First published in 1917, before 1931; the original work is public domain in the United States.).

## Summary

Williams relocates the pastoral from ideal countryside to an urban pavement. Sparrows, a gutter worker, and a minister become subjects for a poem about ordinary value.[1]

```
The little sparrows
hop ingenuously
about the pavement
```

## Meaning and interpretation

The poem reverses social and poetic hierarchy. Useful labor appears more majestic than ceremony, while the ending preserves astonishment instead of a final doctrine.[2]

```
his tread
is more majestic than
that of the Episcopal minister
```

## Themes

### Meaning and interpretation

The poem reverses social and poetic hierarchy. Useful labor appears more majestic than ceremony, while the ending preserves astonishment instead of a final doctrine.[1]

### Form and language

This is a single-stanza free-verse poem whose short lines and enjambment control pace and emphasis.[2]

## Form and meter

This is a single-stanza free-verse poem whose short lines and enjambment control pace and emphasis.[2]

```
The little sparrows
hop ingenuously
about the pavement
```

## Literary devices

### Imagery and contrast

```
The little sparrows
hop ingenuously
about the pavement
```

Concrete images turn the poem’s central abstraction into a memorable scene.

### Repetition and sound

```

is more majestic than
that of the Episcopal minister
```

Repetition and patterned sound give the argument emotional force and shape the reader’s pace.

## Historical context

The work belongs to the public-domain period identified by its first publication year. Its historical setting and literary conventions inform the interpretation without replacing close reading.[1]

This is a single-stanza free-verse poem whose short lines and enjambment control pace and emphasis.[2]

# Paul Revere’s Ride analysis

Paul Revere’s Ride — Henry Wadsworth Longfellow (1860)

This Paul Revere’s Ride analysis explains its meaning, themes, form, and major literary devices.

Full text from [Full text of Paul Revere’s Ride](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Paul_Revere%27s_Ride). Public domain in the US (First published in 1860, before 1931; the original work is public domain in the United States.).

## Summary

Longfellow turns a Revolutionary warning into a national myth. The ride becomes a story about civic attention, courage, and the transmission of memory.[1]

```
Listen, my children, and you shall hear
Of the midnight ride of Paul Revere,
On the eighteenth of April, in Seventy-five;
```

## Meaning and interpretation

The poem is powerful as symbolic history, not as a complete factual account. Its galloping rhythm and final prophecy make Revere an emblem of action in national danger.[2]

```
The fate of a nation was riding that night;
And the spark struck out by that steed, in his flight,
Kindled the land into flame with its heat.
```

## Themes

### Meaning and interpretation

The poem is powerful as symbolic history, not as a complete factual account. Its galloping rhythm and final prophecy make Revere an emblem of action in national danger.[1]

### Form and language

The narrative uses irregular stanzas, steady rhyme, direct address, and predominantly anapestic, galloping movement.[2]

## Form and meter

The narrative uses irregular stanzas, steady rhyme, direct address, and predominantly anapestic, galloping movement.[2]

```
Listen, my children, and you shall hear
Of the midnight ride of Paul Revere,
On the eighteenth of April, in Seventy-five;
```

## Literary devices

### Imagery and contrast

```
Listen, my children, and you shall hear
Of the midnight ride of Paul Revere,
On the eighteenth of April, in Seventy-five;
```

Concrete images turn the poem’s central abstraction into a memorable scene.

### Repetition and sound

```
The fate of a nation was riding that night;
And the spark struck out by that steed, in his flight,
Kindled the land into flame with its heat.
```

Repetition and patterned sound give the argument emotional force and shape the reader’s pace.

## Historical context

The work belongs to the public-domain period identified by its first publication year. Its historical setting and literary conventions inform the interpretation without replacing close reading.[1]

The narrative uses irregular stanzas, steady rhyme, direct address, and predominantly anapestic, galloping movement.[2]

The poem’s meaning emerges from its central images, its treatment of change or conflict, and the relationship between the speaker and the world.

### What are the main themes in Paul Revere’s Ride?

Its main themes include interpretation, human experience, and the way poetic form gives those concerns shape.

# Perplexed Music analysis

Perplexed Music — Elizabeth Barrett Browning (1844)

This Perplexed Music analysis explains its meaning, themes, form, and major literary devices.

Full text from [Full text of Perplexed Music](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Papers_on_Literature_and_Art_%28Fuller%29/Part_II/Chapter_2). Public domain in the US (First published in 1844, before 1931; the original work is public domain in the United States.).

## Summary

The poem compares experience to a musician whose difficult harmonies represent a divine order humans cannot yet hear. Angels perceive the completed cadence behind apparent discord.[1]

```
Experience, like a pale musician, holds
A dulcimer of patience in his hand:
Whence harmonies we cannot understand
```

## Meaning and interpretation

Browning does not deny suffering; she makes limited perspective central to faith. The final “SWEET” reframes pain without pretending that present notes are easy to hear.[2]

```
But angels leaning from the golden seat,
Are not so minded; their fine ear hath won
The issue of completed cadences;
```

## Themes

### Meaning and interpretation

Browning does not deny suffering; she makes limited perspective central to faith. The final “SWEET” reframes pain without pretending that present notes are easy to hear.[1]

### Form and language

This fourteen-line sonnet-like lyric uses an octave and sestet, chiefly iambic pentameter, and a musical metaphor for meaning.[2]

## Form and meter

This fourteen-line sonnet-like lyric uses an octave and sestet, chiefly iambic pentameter, and a musical metaphor for meaning.[2]

```
Experience, like a pale musician, holds
A dulcimer of patience in his hand:
Whence harmonies we cannot understand
```

## Literary devices

### Imagery and contrast

```
Experience, like a pale musician, holds
A dulcimer of patience in his hand:
Whence harmonies we cannot understand
```

Concrete images turn the poem’s central abstraction into a memorable scene.

### Repetition and sound

```
But angels leaning from the golden seat,
Are not so minded; their fine ear hath won
The issue of completed cadences;
```

Repetition and patterned sound give the argument emotional force and shape the reader’s pace.

## Historical context

The work belongs to the public-domain period identified by its first publication year. Its historical setting and literary conventions inform the interpretation without replacing close reading.[1]

This fourteen-line sonnet-like lyric uses an octave and sestet, chiefly iambic pentameter, and a musical metaphor for meaning.[2]

# Richard Cory analysis

Richard Cory — Edwin Arlington Robinson (1897)

This Richard Cory analysis examines how Robinson uses a collective speaker, regular quatrains, and a sudden ending to question the appearance of happiness.

Full text from [Richard Cory](https://poets.org/poem/richard-cory). Public domain in the US (First published in The Children of the Night (1897), before the US public-domain cutoff.).

## Summary

The townspeople describe Richard Cory as polished, wealthy, and enviable, then contrast his apparent completeness with their own hunger and labor.

```
Whenever Richard Cory went down town,
We people on the pavement looked at him:
```

The final sentence reveals Cory’s suicide without supplying a cause. The omission makes the community’s confident interpretation of his life look dangerously incomplete.[2]

## Meaning and interpretation

The poem’s irony comes from confusing visible privilege with inner contentment. The collective “we” sees Cory repeatedly, but its admiration turns him into an image instead of a person.[3]

```
In fine, we thought that he was everything
To make us wish that we were in his place.
```

Robinson does not offer a simple explanation for the death. Instead, the abrupt ending exposes how little observers can know from manners, wealth, or appearance.

## Themes

### Appearance and reality

Cory’s immaculate public image is a projection made by the townspeople. The last line separates that image from the private life they never understood.[3]

### Class and envy

```
So on we worked, and waited for the light,
And went without the meat, and cursed the bread;
```

The workers’ deprivation makes Cory seem to possess the answer to every problem, even though the poem shows that material status is not a complete measure of happiness.

### Failed recognition

The communal speaker watches Cory but never speaks with him about fear, loneliness, or desire. The poem is therefore also about the limits of social knowledge.

## Form and meter

“Richard Cory” is a sixteen-line narrative poem in four quatrains, generally in iambic pentameter. Its regular ABAB pattern makes the town’s assumptions sound orderly.

The controlled form intensifies the shock of the final line: the poem’s calm surface cannot contain what it suddenly reports.[2]

## Literary devices

### Dramatic irony

```
And Richard Cory, one calm summer night,
Went home and put a bullet through his head.
```

The townspeople’s belief that Cory has everything worth wanting becomes tragically ironic when the reader learns how their portrait ends.

### Collective speaker

```
We people on the pavement looked at him:
```

The repeated communal viewpoint makes the poem a study of social perception as much as a character sketch.

### Juxtaposition

Cory’s wealth and refinement are placed beside the workers’ hunger. The contrast explains envy while questioning the community’s definition of success.

## Historical context

Robinson published the poem in The Children of the Night in 1897. Its public-domain text is preserved by the Academy of American Poets.[1]

The poem’s small-town social viewpoint turns class difference into a psychological problem: public admiration and private suffering remain radically separated.

## What critics say

> “The poem may be read as an ironic commentary on the American dream.”
>
> — [Encyclopedia.com](https://www.encyclopedia.com/arts/educational-magazines/richard-cory)

> “The poem's thematic interests in wealth, poverty, and the elusive nature of happiness”
>
> — [LitCharts](https://www.litcharts.com/poetry/edwin-arlington-robinson/richard-cory)

## Common questions

### What is the main meaning of “Richard Cory”?

The poem warns that wealth and a polished public image do not reveal a person’s inner life.

### Why is the ending shocking?

A measured portrait of an enviable man ends with a blunt account of suicide, overturning the observers’ assumptions.

### What is the poem’s form?

It has four quatrains, an ABAB rhyme pattern, and generally iambic-pentameter lines.

## References

- [Academy of American Poets](https://poets.org/poem/richard-cory)

- [Encyclopedia.com](https://www.encyclopedia.com/arts/educational-magazines/richard-cory)

- [LitCharts](https://www.litcharts.com/poetry/edwin-arlington-robinson/richard-cory)

- [Wikisource](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/The_Children_of_the_Night_(1921)/Richard_Cory)

## Open the editor

Write with this poem’s meter in the editor: https://lyriic.com/write/iambic-pentameter

# She Walks in Beauty analysis

She Walks in Beauty — Lord Byron (1815)

This analysis explains how Byron joins physical beauty to inner peace through balanced images of darkness and light.

Full text from [She Walks in Beauty](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poems/43844/she-walks-in-beauty). Public domain in the US (Written in 1814 and published in Hebrew Melodies (1815), before the US public-domain cutoff.).

## Summary

The speaker compares a woman’s beauty to a clear, starry night, where darkness and brightness meet in a gentle balance.

```
She walks in beauty, like the night
Of cloudless climes and starry skies;
```

The poem moves from hair, face, and color toward thought, goodness, peace, and innocent love.[3]

## Meaning and interpretation

Night is not presented as an absence of beauty. Its darkness makes possible a tender light that daylight, described as “gaudy,” cannot provide.

```
One shade the more, one ray the less,
Had half impaired the nameless grace
```

The ideal depends on proportion: either excess shade or excess brightness would damage the harmony. Appearance becomes meaningful because it seems to express a peaceful mind.[1]

## Themes

### Harmony of opposites

Dark and bright, night and light, meet without canceling one another. Contrast is the condition of the poem’s ideal beauty.[1]

### Outer beauty and inner character

```
Where thoughts serenely sweet express,
How pure, how dear their dwelling-place.
```

The speaker gradually moves beneath physical description to moral and emotional qualities.

### Nature and perception

Stars, clouds, night, and light supply a language for describing beauty as a changing relation rather than a fixed list of features.

## Form and meter

The lyric has three six-line stanzas with an ABABAB rhyme scheme. Its alternating iambic tetrameter and trimeter create the familiar movement of common meter.

Regular stanza shape and balanced clauses enact the harmony the speaker praises.[3]

## Literary devices

### Simile

```
She walks in beauty, like the night
```

The opening comparison makes night a positive image and immediately establishes the poem’s preference for softened darkness.

### Antithesis

```
And all that’s best of dark and bright
Meet in her aspect and her eyes;
```

Paired opposites organize the claim that beauty is created by a measured combination of qualities.

### Personification

```
Which heaven to gaudy day denies.
```

Heaven appears to withhold a tender quality from daylight, giving the preference for night a cosmic scale.

## Historical context

Byron dated the poem June 12, 1814; it appeared in Hebrew Melodies in 1815. The Wikisource edition preserves a note connecting its inspiration with Anne Beatrix Wilmot’s mourning dress and spangles.[3]

The lyric’s compact, singable stanzas also reflect its setting within a collection designed to be paired with music.

## What critics say

> “And all that’s best of dark and bright / Meet in her aspect and her eyes”
>
> — [Poetry Foundation](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poems/43844/she-walks-in-beauty)

> “One shade the more, one ray the less, / Had half impaired the nameless grace”
>
> — [Wikisource](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/The_Works_of_Lord_Byron_(ed._Coleridge,_Prothero)/Poetry/Volume_3/Hebrew_Melodies/She_walks_in_Beauty)

## Common questions

### What is the main meaning?

Beauty is presented as a harmony of light and darkness joined to inner peace, goodness, and innocent love.

### What does night symbolize?

Night represents a gentle, restrained light and the balance that makes the speaker’s ideal beauty possible.

### What is the form and meter?

The poem has three six-line stanzas, ABABAB rhyme, and mainly alternating iambic tetrameter and trimeter.

## References

- [Academy of American Poets](https://poets.org/poem/she-walks-beauty)

- [Poetry Foundation](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poems/43844/she-walks-in-beauty)

- [Wikisource](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/The_Works_of_Lord_Byron_(ed._Coleridge,_Prothero)/Poetry/Volume_3/Hebrew_Melodies/She_walks_in_Beauty)

- [Poetry Foundation, Hebrew Melodies](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poems/43844/she-walks-in-beauty)

## Open the editor

Write with this poem’s meter in the editor: https://lyriic.com/write/common-meter

# Song of Myself analysis

Song of Myself — Walt Whitman (1855)

Whitman’s Song of Myself turns a personal voice into an expansive claim about shared human identity. This analysis focuses on its meaning, themes, and free verse.

Full text from [Leaves of Grass (1855), “I celebrate myself”](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Leaves_of_Grass_(1855)/I_celebrate_myself). Public domain in the US (First published as “I celebrate myself” in Leaves of Grass (1855), before the US public-domain cutoff.).

## Summary

The speaker celebrates himself while immediately linking his identity to the reader. The poem’s “I” expands through bodies, work, nature, death, and shared experience.

```
I celebrate myself,
And what I assume you shall assume,
```

When a child asks what grass means, the speaker offers several guesses rather than a final definition. The poem keeps knowledge open and experiential.[2]

## Meaning and interpretation

Whitman’s self-celebration is not meant to isolate the speaker. “Every atom” becomes a material image of equality between poet and reader.

```
For every atom belonging to me as good belongs to you.
```

Grass gathers possible meanings—common life, spiritual mystery, and continuity between the living and the dead—without settling into one symbol.[3]

## Themes

### Self and shared identity

The singular voice becomes a route into fellowship: the speaker asks readers to recognize their own material and spiritual participation in the world.

### Democracy and equality

Catalogues place bodies, occupations, places, and experiences in an expansive series. Formally and thematically, the poem resists a narrow hierarchy of subjects.[2]

### Nature and mystery

```
I lean and loafe at my ease .... observing a spear of summer grass.
```

Ordinary natural objects become occasions for thought, not decorations placed outside human experience.

## Form and meter

The poem uses free verse rather than a fixed meter or regular rhyme scheme. Breath-length lines, parallel syntax, anaphora, and catalogues supply its rhythm.

James E. Miller argues that the poem’s apparent looseness should not be mistaken for the absence of structure; he searches for an informing idea connecting its parts.[2]

## Literary devices

### Anaphora

```
I celebrate myself,
And what I assume you shall assume,
```

Repeated conjunctions and openings create additive forward motion, making each perception part of an unfinished whole.

### Catalogue

Whitman’s long lists widen the field of attention and give equality a formal shape by placing unlike people and sensations in one sequence.

### Symbolism

```
I guess it must be the flag of my disposition, out of hopeful green stuff woven.
```

Grass remains multivalent: it can suggest character, growth, divine communication, and shared material life.

## Historical context

Whitman self-published Leaves of Grass on July 4, 1855. The poem was initially untitled, and later editions changed its title, wording, and section divisions.[3]

The first edition’s democratic address and long lines helped establish Whitman’s distinct American poetic voice. The Poetry Foundation describes his method as adapting epic scale through connected lyric poems.[3]

## What critics say

> “Inability to find a structure in “Song of Myself” has resulted, I believe, from a failure to find a center of relevancy, an “informing idea,” to which the parts of the poem may be related.”
>
> — James E. Miller Jr., [PMLA / Cambridge Core](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/pmla/article/abs/song-of-myself-as-inverted-mystical-experience/A58A45564DC5E54D10E98CB71E56E1AB)

> “Whitman adapted the form of the epic, constructing it by connecting lyric poems; the long, narrative lines in “Song of Myself” are characteristic of his poetry.”
>
> — [Poetry Foundation](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/articles/69391/from-preface-to-leaves-of-grass-first-edition)

## Common questions

### What is the main meaning?

Whitman presents individuality as connected to other people, the natural world, and shared material life.

### What does grass symbolize?

Grass has several possible meanings, including common life, spiritual mystery, growth, and continuity between living and dead bodies.

### What form does the poem use?

It uses free verse, with rhythm shaped by breath, syntax, repetition, and catalogues rather than fixed meter.

## References

- [Wikisource](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Leaves_of_Grass_(1855)/I_celebrate_myself)

- [James E. Miller Jr., PMLA / Cambridge Core](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/pmla/article/abs/song-of-myself-as-inverted-mystical-experience/A58A45564DC5E54D10E98CB71E56E1AB)

- [Poetry Foundation](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/articles/69391/from-preface-to-leaves-of-grass-first-edition)

- [Poetry Foundation](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/articles/69391/from-preface-to-leaves-of-grass-first-edition)

## Open the editor

Open the zen editor: https://lyriic.com/write

# Song of the Witches analysis

Song of the Witches — William Shakespeare (1606)

This analysis explains how “Double, double, toil and trouble” turns a grotesque ingredient list into a ritual of disorder.

Full text from [Macbeth, Act IV, Scene I](https://www.shakespeare-online.com/plays/macbeth_4_1.html). Public domain in the US (Macbeth was written and performed in the early seventeenth century; Shakespeare’s text is public domain.).

## Summary

Three witches prepare a potion from poisonous animals, plants, and human remains. The recurring refrain makes the inventory sound like a spell.

```
Round about the cauldron go;
In the poison’d entrails throw.
```

The chant occurs as Macbeth seeks supernatural knowledge, so its organized recipe gives physical form to a world of moral corruption.[2]

## Meaning and interpretation

“Double” suggests intensification and doubleness: the refrain is catchy and musical while the witches’ language elsewhere hides danger inside apparent certainty.

```
Double, double toil and trouble;
Fire burn and cauldron bubble.
```

The chant does not merely describe magic; repetition, rhyme, and falling rhythm perform a ritual that makes disorder feel controlled.[3]

## Themes

### Chaos made ritual

Imperatives such as throw, boil, add, and cool impose sequence on grotesque materials. The witches give supernatural disorder the shape of a recipe.

### Deception and doubleness

```
For a charm of powerful trouble,
Like a hell-broth boil and bubble.
```

The sing-song surface disguises destructive purpose, echoing the witches’ misleading prophecies.

### Corrupted nature

Animal parts and plants are stripped of ordinary identity and reduced to ingredients, making the natural world raw material for violence.

## Form and meter

The chant is mainly trochaic tetrameter, often catalectic, with four falling beats and a clipped ending. Rhyming couplets separate the witches’ speech from the play’s usual blank verse.[3]

The repeated “trouble / bubble” rhyme makes the spell circular and memorable.

## Literary devices

### Refrain

```
Double, double toil and trouble;
Fire burn and cauldron bubble.
```

Returning after each ingredient group makes the incantation feel iterative, as though each cycle increases its force.

### Catalogue

```
Eye of newt and toe of frog,
Wool of bat and tongue of dog,
```

Paired body parts accumulate sensory detail while reducing living creatures to interchangeable components.

### Grotesque imagery

```
Finger of birth-strangled babe
Ditch-deliver’d by a drab,
```

The movement from animal parts to human remains makes the magic ethically repellent, not merely exotic.

## Historical context

Macbeth was written around 1606 during James I’s reign, when witchcraft, treason, kingship, and supernatural signs were powerful cultural concerns.

The early modern text contains antisemitic and dehumanizing language in its ingredient list. That historical wording should be identified critically rather than repeated as neutral description.[2]

## What critics say

> “The witches' chant uses trochaic tetrameter (strong/weak pattern, four times) with catalectic lines (missing the final weak syllable).”
>
> — [The Educational Hub](https://educationalhub.org/shakespeare-macbeth-witches-reading-analysis/)

> “The speeches of the witches are thrown into the same trochaic metre that they have employed on their former appearances.”
>
> — [Shakespeare Online](https://www.shakespeare-online.com/plays/macbeth_4_1.html)

## Common questions

### What does “Double, double, toil and trouble” mean?

It is an incantation that intensifies the witches’ work and hints at the deceptive doubleness of their language.

### What meter does the chant use?

It mainly uses catalectic trochaic tetrameter and rhyming couplets.

### Why list strange ingredients?

The catalogue turns violence into a physical recipe and creates grotesque sensory imagery.

## References

- [Academy of American Poets](https://poets.org/poem/macbeth-act-iv-scene-i-round-about-cauldron-go)

- [Shakespeare Online](https://www.shakespeare-online.com/plays/macbeth_4_1.html)

- [The Educational Hub](https://educationalhub.org/shakespeare-macbeth-witches-reading-analysis/)

- [No Sweat Shakespeare](https://nosweatshakespeare.com/quotes/famous/double-double-toil-and-trouble/)

## Open the editor

Write with this poem’s meter in the editor: https://lyriic.com/write/trochaic-tetrameter

# Sonnet 73 analysis

Sonnet 73 — William Shakespeare (1609)

This Sonnet 73 analysis explains how three diminishing images turn aging into an argument for intensified love.

Full text from [Sonnet 73](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poems/45099/sonnet-73-that-time-of-year-thou-mayst-in-me-behold). Public domain in the US (Shakespeare’s Sonnets were first published in 1609 and are public domain.).

## Summary

The speaker asks the beloved to see him as late autumn, fading twilight, and a fire nearly consumed by its own fuel.[1]

```
That time of year thou mayst in me behold
When yellow leaves, or none, or few, do hang
```

The final couplet turns decline into an emotional claim: awareness of approaching separation makes love stronger.[2]

## Meaning and interpretation

The metaphors narrow in scale from a season to a day and then to the last glow of a fire. Mortality becomes increasingly immediate.

```
In me thou see’st the glowing of such fire
That on the ashes of his youth doth lie,
```

The couplet makes impermanence part of love’s value. What must soon be left is cherished more carefully now.[2]

## Themes

### Aging and mortality

Sparse leaves, vanishing light, and dying embers make bodily decline visible. “Death’s second self” joins ordinary sleep to mortality.

### Time and compression

```
Which by and by black night doth take away,
Death’s second self, that seals up all in rest.
```

Each quatrain measures a smaller remainder of time, compressing the speaker’s future.

### Love strengthened by loss

The closing argument is paradoxical: the beloved’s knowledge of impending separation intensifies attachment.

## Form and meter

This is a Shakespearean sonnet: three quatrains and a couplet, with ABAB CDCD EFEF GG rhyme and chiefly iambic pentameter.

The repeated “In me thou see’st” creates parallel structure, while the couplet turns image into conclusion.

## Literary devices

### Extended metaphor

```
In me thou see’st the twilight of such day
As after sunset fadeth in the west,
```

Autumn, twilight, and fire are successive versions of the same approach toward disappearance.

### Personification

```
Which by and by black night doth take away
```

Night acts as an agent that removes the remaining light, giving death an unavoidable force.

### Paradox

```
This thou perceiv’st, which makes thy love more strong,
To love that well which thou must leave ere long.
```

Weakening and approaching loss produce stronger love, making mortality emotionally productive.

## Historical context

The sonnets appeared in the 1609 Quarto. Sonnet 73 is traditionally associated with the Fair Youth sequence, though the poems do not establish a complete biography.

The poem’s “ruin’d choirs” can evoke both bare branches and stripped church interiors, layering personal aging with cultural memory.[2]

## What critics say

> “The fundamental emotion [in Sonnet 73] is self-pity. Not an attractive emotion. What renders it pathetic, in the good instead of the bad sense, is the sinister diminution of the time concept, quatrain by quatrain.”
>
> — John Berryman, [Shakespeare Online](https://www.shakespeare-online.com/sonnets/73detail.html)

> “The structure is good, the three quatrains offering distinct yet equivalent figures for the time of life of the unsuccessful and to-be-pitied lover.”
>
> — John Crowe Ransom, [Shakespeare Online](https://www.shakespeare-online.com/sonnets/73detail.html)

## Common questions

### What is the main meaning?

Three images of decline lead to the idea that approaching loss can make love more intense.

### What are the three metaphors?

The speaker compares himself to late autumn, fading twilight, and a dying fire.

### What is the form?

It is a Shakespearean sonnet in iambic pentameter with ABAB CDCD EFEF GG rhyme.

## References

- [Poetry Foundation](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poems/45099/sonnet-73-that-time-of-year-thou-mayst-in-me-behold)

- [John Berryman, Shakespeare Online](https://www.shakespeare-online.com/sonnets/73detail.html)

- [John Crowe Ransom, Shakespeare Online](https://www.shakespeare-online.com/sonnets/73detail.html)

- [Wikisource](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Shakespeare%27s_Sonnets)

## Open the editor

Write with this poem’s meter in the editor: https://lyriic.com/write/sonnet

# Stopping by Woods on a Snowy Evening analysis

Stopping by Woods on a Snowy Evening — Robert Frost (1923)

This analysis examines the poem’s quiet scene, interlocking rhyme, and unresolved pull between the woods and the speaker’s obligations.

Full text from [Stopping by Woods on a Snowy Evening](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/New_Hampshire,_a_Poem_with_Notes_and_Grace_Notes/Stopping_by_Woods_on_a_Snowy_Evening). Public domain in the US (First published in New Hampshire (1923), before the US public-domain cutoff.).

## Summary

A traveler pauses to watch snow fill privately owned woods. His horse interrupts the stillness, and the speaker remembers promises and distance.

```
The woods are lovely, dark and deep.
But I have promises to keep,
```

The repeated closing line can describe ordinary travel while also suggesting a darker meditation on sleep and death.[3]

## Meaning and interpretation

The poem lets beauty and duty coexist. The woods offer solitude and rest, while promises bind the speaker to people and responsibilities outside the scene.

```
And miles to go before I sleep,
And miles to go before I sleep.
```

The poem does not force a single interpretation: the final repetition may sound like resolve, weariness, self-command, or a thought lingering near sleep.[2]

## Themes

### Duty and temptation

The speaker is drawn toward the woods but turns toward obligations. The pause is meaningful precisely because it is not allowed to become permanent.

### Nature and society

```
He will not see me stopping here
To watch his woods fill up with snow.
```

Ownership, village, farmhouse, horse, and harness bells place the speaker between society and a nearly silent landscape.

### Rest and mortality

Darkness, snow, and sleep support both a literal travel reading and a suggestive meditation on death.[2]

## Form and meter

The poem has four quatrains in iambic tetrameter. Its chain rhyme is AABA BBCB CCDC DDDD, with each third line preparing the next stanza’s rhyme.

The final stanza resolves into one repeated rhyme, making formal closure sound like an echo rather than a simple ending.[3]

## Literary devices

### Personification

```
My little horse must think it queer
To stop without a farmhouse near
```

The speaker imagines the horse judging the unexplained stop, giving practical society a nearby voice.

### Sensory imagery

```
The only other sound’s the sweep
Of easy wind and downy flake.
```

Soft sound and touch make the snow sheltering, which also makes the woods’ darkness more seductive.

### Repetition

```
And miles to go before I sleep
```

Repeating the line turns a travel statement into an unresolved verbal echo.[3]

## Historical context

Frost wrote the poem in 1922 and published it in New Hampshire in 1923. The Wikisource text preserves the poem’s public-domain form.

Its traditional form and plain rural setting allow philosophical tension to emerge through ordinary speech rather than abstract argument.

## What critics say

> “Though Frost’s poem resists a definitive interpretation, the natural world it depicts is at once “lovely” and overwhelming.”
>
> — [LitCharts](https://www.litcharts.com/poetry/robert-frost/stopping-by-woods-on-a-snowy-evening)

> “The basic conflict in the poem, resolved in the last stanza, is between an attraction toward the woods and the pull of responsibility outside of the woods.”
>
> — [SparkNotes](https://www.sparknotes.com/poetry/frost/section10/)

## Common questions

### What is the main meaning?

The speaker is tempted by a beautiful, dark pause but pulled onward by promises and responsibilities.

### What do the final miles mean?

Literally they are travel before rest; figuratively they can suggest unfinished duties before death, though the poem remains open.

### What is the rhyme and meter?

It uses iambic tetrameter and interlocking AABA BBCB CCDC DDDD rhyme.

## References

- [Wikisource](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/New_Hampshire,_a_Poem_with_Notes_and_Grace_Notes/Stopping_by_Woods_on_a_Snowy_Evening)

- [LitCharts](https://www.litcharts.com/poetry/robert-frost/stopping-by-woods-on-a-snowy-evening)

- [SparkNotes](https://www.sparknotes.com/poetry/frost/section10/)

- [Academy of American Poets](https://poets.org/poem/stopping-woods-snowy-evening)

## Open the editor

Write with this poem’s meter in the editor: https://lyriic.com/write/iambic-tetrameter

# The Ballad of the Harp-Weaver analysis

The Ballad of the Harp-Weaver — Edna St. Vincent Millay (1922)

This analysis explains how a mother’s magical gift exposes the costs of poverty, care, and gendered labor.

Full text from [The Ballad of the Harp-Weaver](https://poets.org/poem/ballad-harp-weaver). Public domain in the US (First published in 1922, before the US public-domain cutoff.).

## Summary

A poor mother has no cloth, food, or fuel for her son. On Christmas Eve she uses her harp to weave him warm clothing.

```
“Son,” said my mother,
When I was knee-high,
“You’ve need of clothes to cover you,
```

The child wakes to find the clothes beside his mother, whose hands are frozen in the harp-strings. The miracle is inseparable from its cost.[3]

## Meaning and interpretation

Maternal love is inventive and immense, but the poem refuses to make sacrifice uncomplicated. The clothing saves the child while revealing the conditions that consume the person providing care.

```
She sang as she worked,
And the harp-strings spoke;
Her voice never faltered,
```

The harp changes from an object nobody will buy into an instrument of creation, making neglected artistic power visible.[3]

## Themes

### Maternal love and sacrifice

The mother turns her last strength into protection, and the miraculous clothing makes the fatal cost of that care visible.

### Poverty and neglect

```
Men say the winter
Was bad that year;
Fuel was scarce,
```

The repeated lack of clothing, food, and fuel makes private love carry a burden that society has failed to share.

### Women’s labor and art

The mother is musician and weaver, but her creative identity is recognized only when it serves the child.[3]

## Form and meter

The poem is a narrative ballad in thirty mostly quatrain stanzas, with a largely ABCB rhyme pattern and flexible accentual rhythm.

Repetition and sound effects—“She wove,” “Looking nineteen,” and “weav-weav-weaving”—make the story feel oral and song-like.[3]

## Literary devices

### Personification

```
A wind with a wolf’s head
Howled about our door
```

The wolf-headed wind makes winter an active predator and intensifies the family’s isolation.

### Symbolism

```
And a harp with a woman’s head
Nobody will buy
```

The harp represents the mother’s neglected creative identity before becoming the source of survival.

### Irony

```
Were the clothes of a king’s son,
Just my size.
```

Regal clothing appears in a house without food or fuel, making triumph and loss occupy the same image.

## Historical context

The poem was first published in 1922 and later gave its name to Millay’s Pulitzer Prize-winning collection. The Academy of American Poets identifies it as public domain.[1]

Its traditional ballad frame places a poor mother and child inside a fairy-tale structure, then makes the miracle inseparable from class deprivation and gendered labor.

## What critics say

> “The theme of ‘The Ballad of the Harp-Weaver’ is the enduring strength of a mother’s love.”
>
> — [Poem Analysis](https://poemanalysis.com/edna-st-vincent-millay/the-ballad-of-the-harp-weaver/)

> “The “Ballad of the Harp-Weaver” is Edna Millay’s loud outcry against the traditional role of women in society.”
>
> — [The Tina Edit](https://thetinaedit.com/poem-analysis-of-the-ballad-of-the-harp-weaver-by-edna-st-vincent-millay/)

## Common questions

### What is the meaning?

The poem portrays maternal love as creative and powerful while showing that survival depends on a devastating sacrifice made under poverty.

### Why does the mother die?

She spends the cold night weaving clothes for her son, and her hands are frozen in the harp-strings by morning.

### What does the harp symbolize?

It represents neglected artistic identity and the creative power that transforms music into protection.

## References

- [Academy of American Poets](https://poets.org/poem/ballad-harp-weaver)

- [Poetry Foundation](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poems/53241/the-ballad-of-the-harp-weaver)

- [Poem Analysis](https://poemanalysis.com/edna-st-vincent-millay/the-ballad-of-the-harp-weaver/)

- [The Tina Edit](https://thetinaedit.com/poem-analysis-of-the-ballad-of-the-harp-weaver-by-edna-st-vincent-millay/)

## Open the editor

Write with this poem’s ballad rhythm in the editor: https://lyriic.com/write

# The Battle Hymn of the Republic analysis

The Battle Hymn of the Republic — Julia Ward Howe (1862)

This analysis explains how Julia Ward Howe turns a marching song into a religious vision of justice, war, sacrifice, and freedom.

Full text from [The Battle Hymn of the Republic](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/The_Atlantic_Monthly/Battle_Hymn_of_the_Republic). Public domain in the US (First published in The Atlantic Monthly in February 1862, before the US public-domain cutoff.).

## Summary

The speaker sees Civil War camps, weapons, trumpets, and marching feet as signs that divine judgment is moving through history.[1]

```
Mine eyes have seen the glory of the coming of the Lord:
He is trampling out the vintage where the grapes of wrath are stored;
```

The hymn moves from judgment toward a demand that people die to make others free.[2]

## Meaning and interpretation

The poem frames the Union cause and emancipation as part of a sacred drama. Truth is imagined as an active force moving through armies, sacrifice, and history.

```
As He died to make men holy, let us die to make men free,
While God is marching on.
```

That framing is hopeful but severe: freedom is holy, yet the path toward it involves judgment and human cost.[2]

## Themes

### Justice and judgment

The Lord reads hearts and answers people according to how they treat those they contemn. Confidence in justice includes a threat of reckoning.

### Emancipation and action

```
With a glory in his bosom that transfigures you and me:
```

Christ’s sacrifice becomes a model for people willing to act so others can be free.

### War as sacred history

Military spectacle is transformed into biblical sign, interpreting the Civil War as a crisis in the nation’s moral direction.[2]

## Form and meter

The poem has five four-line stanzas with hymn-like 8.7.8.7 movement, flexible stresses, and an ABCB-like rhyme pattern.

Its repeated marching refrain and connection with the tune of “John Brown’s Body” make collective performance central to its effect.[2]

## Literary devices

### Biblical allusion

```
He is trampling out the vintage where the grapes of wrath are stored;
```

The vintage and grapes of wrath evoke prophetic judgment and give the war an absolute moral scale.

### Extended metaphor

```
I have read a fiery gospel writ in burnished rows of steel:
```

Rows of weapons become a gospel, fusing military spectacle with scriptural interpretation.

### Personification

```
His truth is marching on.
```

Truth receives the movement of an army or procession, becoming active and historical.

## Historical context

Howe wrote the poem in November 1861 after hearing Union soldiers sing “John Brown’s Body.” It appeared on the first page of The Atlantic Monthly in February 1862.[2]

Florence Howe Hall records that James T. Fields supplied the title and that the poem quickly circulated through newspapers, army hymnbooks, and broadsides.

## What critics say

> “The passion of the poem seems, indeed, to lift on high and glorify our poor humanity.”
>
> — Florence Marion Howe Hall, [The Story of the Battle Hymn of the Republic](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/The_Story_of_the_Battle_Hymn_of_the_Republic/Chapter_4)

> “The original draft of the “Battle Hymn” was written on the back of a sheet of the letter-paper of the Sanitary Commission”
>
> — [The Story of the Battle Hymn of the Republic](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/The_Story_of_the_Battle_Hymn_of_the_Republic/Chapter_4)

## Common questions

### What is the main meaning?

The poem interprets the Civil War as a sacred struggle in which judgment moves toward freedom.

### What are its main themes?

Judgment, emancipation, sacrifice, religious faith, and the attempt to understand war as moral history.

### What is its form?

It is a five-stanza hymn with four lines per stanza, flexible 8.7.8.7 movement, rhyme, and repeated refrains.

## References

- [Wikisource](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/The_Atlantic_Monthly/Battle_Hymn_of_the_Republic)

- [Florence Marion Howe Hall, The Story of the Battle Hymn of the Republic](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/The_Story_of_the_Battle_Hymn_of_the_Republic/Chapter_4)

- [The Story of the Battle Hymn of the Republic](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/The_Story_of_the_Battle_Hymn_of_the_Republic/Chapter_4)

- [The Atlantic Monthly](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/The_Atlantic_Monthly/Battle_Hymn_of_the_Republic)

## Open the editor

Write with this poem’s meter in the editor: https://lyriic.com/write

# The Charge of the Light Brigade analysis

The Charge of the Light Brigade — Alfred, Lord Tennyson (1854)

This analysis explains how Tennyson makes a disastrous Crimean War charge into a ballad of courage, obedience, error, and memory.

Full text from [The Charge of the Light Brigade](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/The_Charge_of_the_Light_Brigade_(Tennyson)). Public domain in the US (First published in The Examiner on December 9, 1854, before the US public-domain cutoff.).

## Summary

The poem narrates the brigade’s advance into artillery fire, its sabre attack, and the reduced group returning through the same danger.

```
Half a league, half a league,
Half a league onward,
All in the valley of Death
```

Tennyson praises the soldiers while keeping the command’s mistake visible. The final imperative turns the charge into public memory.[2]

## Meaning and interpretation

The central tension is between obedience and judgment. The soldiers act despite knowing that someone has blundered, while the poem leaves responsibility for the disaster in view.

```
Their’s not to make reply,
Their’s not to reason why,
Their’s but to do and die:
```

The valley, jaws, and mouth of Hell make the route mythic without erasing bodily loss. The ending honors courage, not the wisdom of the order.[2]

## Themes

### Duty and obedience

The poem separates command from action: soldiers obey even when judgment has failed. That division honors discipline while exposing its danger.

### Courage and sacrifice

```
While horse and hero fell,
They that had fought so well
```

Praise is directed at the soldiers’ conduct and endurance rather than the decision that sent them into the valley.

### Remembrance

Refrains and repeated numbers turn one battle into communal memory, while “Left of six hundred” makes the cost audible.[2]

## Form and meter

This six-stanza narrative ballad uses short, heavily stressed lines, repeated phrases, and a strongly dactylic, often dactylic-dimeter movement.

The recurring rhymes—hundred, blunder’d, thunder’d, wonder’d, sunder’d—create compulsive motion, while the changed refrain records depletion.[3]

## Literary devices

### Repetition

```
Rode the six hundred.
```

The refrain gives the charge ceremonial momentum; later “Left of six hundred” repeats the sound while changing its meaning.

### Auditory imagery

```
Cannon to right of them,
Cannon to left of them,
Cannon in front of them
```

Symmetrical repetition verbally surrounds the riders, while “volley’d” and “thunder’d” make the artillery audible.

### Understatement

```
Some one had blunder’d.
```

The vague subject and restrained verb place a small phrase beside enormous loss, avoiding a simple assignment of blame.

## Historical context

The poem responds to the Charge of the Light Brigade at Balaklava on October 25, 1854. A misunderstanding sent cavalry toward Russian artillery; Tennyson published the poem in The Examiner on December 9.[2]

Seamus Perry describes the poem as suspended between admiration for the charge’s magnificence and conviction of its idiocy.[2]

## What critics say

> “Tennyson is suspended between admiration at the reckless magnificence of the charge and a conviction of its idiocy.”
>
> — Seamus Perry, [Victorian Poetry and Poetics](https://odp.library.tamu.edu/victorianpoetry/chapter/seamus-perry-the-charge-of-the-light-brigade-making-poetry-from-war/)

> “Not a protest, but in no way a celebration of a disastrous historical event, it remains a compelling dramatisation of battle”
>
> — [The Guardian](https://www.theguardian.com/books/booksblog/2014/jan/20/poem-of-the-week-charge-light-brigade-tennyson)

## Common questions

### What is the meaning?

The poem honors courage and obedience during a disastrous charge without hiding the military error.

### What are the themes?

Duty, courage, sacrifice, military error, and remembrance.

### What is the meter?

It is a short-line ballad with strongly dactylic, galloping rhythm and repeated rhymes.

## References

- [Wikisource](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/The_Charge_of_the_Light_Brigade_(Tennyson))

- [Seamus Perry, Victorian Poetry and Poetics](https://odp.library.tamu.edu/victorianpoetry/chapter/seamus-perry-the-charge-of-the-light-brigade-making-poetry-from-war/)

- [The Guardian](https://www.theguardian.com/books/booksblog/2014/jan/20/poem-of-the-week-charge-light-brigade-tennyson)

- [Victorian Poetry and Poetics](https://odp.library.tamu.edu/victorianpoetry/chapter/the-charge-of-the-light-brigade-1854/)

## Open the editor

Write with this poem’s galloping rhythm in the editor: https://lyriic.com/write

# The Cremation of Sam McGee analysis

The Cremation of Sam McGee — Robert W. Service (1907)

This analysis explains how Service turns a grim Yukon promise into a fast-moving narrative of loyalty, survival, and comic reversal.

Full text from [The Cremation of Sam McGee](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/The_Cremation_of_Sam_McGee). Public domain in the US (First published in Songs of a Sourdough (1907), before the US public-domain cutoff.).

## Summary

Sam, terrified of an icy grave, asks Cap to cremate him if he dies on the trail. Cap carries out the promise at Lake Lebarge using a derelict steamer.

```
There are strange things done in the midnight sun
By the men who moil for gold;
```

The horror reverses into comedy when Sam is alive inside the furnace, enjoying its warmth.[3]

## Meaning and interpretation

The poem treats loyalty as a practical law: “a promise made is a debt unpaid” gives Cap’s exhausting task a moral shape.

```
A pal’s last need is a thing to heed,
So I swore I would not fail;
```

The twist does not erase the danger. Its humor grows from the same cold that nearly kills Sam, making warmth a reversal of the Yukon world.[2]

## Themes

### Friendship and loyalty

Cap’s actions are driven by Sam’s request, and the trail’s code turns a private promise into a social duty.

### Survival and landscape

```
Talk of your cold! through the parka’s fold it stabbed like a driven nail.
```

Cold is physical and psychological: it freezes eyelashes, drains the dogs, and turns a companion’s body into a burden.

### Death and dark comedy

Service creates a Gothic situation with a corpse and furnace, then breaks the tension through Sam’s literal complaint about the cold.[2]

## Form and meter

The poem is a narrative ballad framed by a repeated eight-line stanza. Its dominant movement is anapestic tetrameter, varied for conversational speech.

Internal rhyme and paired end rhyme create forward momentum suited to mushing, oral recitation, and a fireside tale.[3]

## Literary devices

### Simile

```
Through the parka’s fold it stabbed like a driven nail.
```

The comparison gives cold the force of a weapon and prepares the reader for Sam’s fear of the icy grave.

### Personification

```
Now a promise made is a debt unpaid, and the trail has its own stern code.
```

The trail becomes an authority, making Cap’s promise part of a culture of survival.

### Irony and reversal

```
Since I left Plumtree, down in Tennessee, it’s the first time I’ve been warm.
```

Sam’s calm response reverses the expected result of cremation: warmth, not death, is the immediate point of the furnace.

## Historical context

The poem appeared in Service’s 1907 collection Songs of a Sourdough, drawing on the Yukon world associated with the Klondike Gold Rush.

Service’s narrative turns a grim survival anecdote into a comic ballad whose moral center is the keeping of a promise.[2]

## What critics say

> “Service uses rhyme and rhythm not only to entertain but to subtly mirror the march of obligation through harsh, unforgiving terrain.”
>
> — Sudip Das Gupta, [Poem Analysis](https://poemanalysis.com/robert-service/the-cremation-of-sam-mcgee/)

> “exhibits the elements that mark Service’s style: internal rhymes, stressed rhythms, a dash of stereotypical Yukon machismo, ironic and slightly macabre humor”
>
> — [Encyclopedia.com](https://www.encyclopedia.com/arts/educational-magazines/cremation-sam-mcgee)

## Common questions

### What is the meaning?

The poem presents friendship as a promise honored under extreme conditions, then transforms fear into dark comedy.

### What are the themes?

Loyalty, survival, gold, death, and comic reversal.

### Is Sam McGee really dead?

No. Cap expects a corpse, but Sam is alive inside the furnace and finally feels warm.

## References

- [Wikisource](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/The_Cremation_of_Sam_McGee)

- [Sudip Das Gupta, Poem Analysis](https://poemanalysis.com/robert-service/the-cremation-of-sam-mcgee/)

- [Encyclopedia.com](https://www.encyclopedia.com/arts/educational-magazines/cremation-sam-mcgee)

- [Internet Archive](https://archive.org/details/songssourdough00servuoft)

## Open the editor

Write with this poem’s rhythm in the editor: https://lyriic.com/write

# The Highwayman analysis

The Highwayman — Alfred Noyes (1906)

This analysis follows Noyes’s doomed lovers through a vivid narrative ballad of betrayal, sacrifice, and legendary return.

Full text from [The Highwayman](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poems/43187/the-highwayman). Public domain in the US (First published in 1906, before the US public-domain cutoff.).

## Summary

A highwayman visits Bess, the landlord’s daughter, and promises to return by moonlight. Tim the ostler, who loves Bess, betrays the meeting to King George’s soldiers.

```
The wind was a torrent of darkness among the gusty trees.
The moon was a ghostly galleon tossed upon cloudy seas.
The road was a ribbon of moonlight over the purple moor.
```

The soldiers use Bess as bait. She fires the musket tied beneath her breast to warn the approaching rider, and the highwayman later rides back in grief and is killed.[2]

## Meaning and interpretation

The poem makes love an active sacrifice rather than a private feeling. Bess’s warning saves the highwayman from the ambush but costs her life; his return turns grief into a second fatal act.[2]

```
Her musket shattered the moonlight,
Shattered her breast in the moonlight and warned him—with her death.
```

The final “they say” moves the lovers from history into legend. The repeated opening images suggest that communal storytelling preserves their bond after both bodies are gone.[3]

## Themes

### Love and sacrifice

Bess chooses a warning that she knows will kill her, while the highwayman’s return shows devotion shaped by loss.

### Betrayal and power

Tim’s jealousy enables the soldiers’ ambush, joining private resentment to institutional violence.

### Memory and legend

The closing winter-night refrain turns tragedy into a story that can be repeated across generations.[3]

## Form and meter

This is a narrative ballad in two parts, with irregular stanza lengths, recurring refrains, dialogue, and a strong performance-like pulse.

Long rolling lines mix iambic and anapaestic movement, while short repeated phrases imitate hoofbeats and marching. The repeated “Riding—riding—” makes motion audible.

## Literary devices

### Metaphor

```
The moon was a ghostly galleon tossed upon cloudy seas.
```

The moon becomes a ship and the clouds a sea, enlarging the road into a mythic night journey.

### Onomatopoeia

```
Tlot-tlot; tlot-tlot! Had they heard it?
```

The invented hoofbeat is both a sound effect and a suspense signal: its return announces love, danger, and approaching death.

### Refrain

```
Look for me by moonlight;
Watch for me by moonlight;
I’ll come to thee by moonlight, though hell should bar the way!
```

The promise is repeated by the soldiers as cruelty and finally survives as a ghostly pattern.

## Historical context

Noyes first published the poem in 1906. Its King George setting supplies historical color, but the poem’s main method is romantic ballad legend rather than documentary history.

The Penn State study describes the poem as a vessel for collective memory, emphasizing how its images and narrative can preserve a period’s imagined past.[3]

## What critics say

> “The poem is notable for the way in which it reverses our expectations concerning light and dark imagery.”
>
> — [Encyclopedia.com](https://www.encyclopedia.com/arts/educational-magazines/highwayman)

> “Alfred Noyes's “The Highwayman” (1906) and Federico García Lorca's “Romance sonámbulo” (1928) ... serve as literary vessels for the collective memory of historical periods.”
>
> — [Penn State, ES Review](https://pure.psu.edu/en/publications/ballads-as-vessels-for-collective-cultural-memory-a-critical-comp/)

## Common questions

### What is the meaning of The Highwayman?

It presents love as courageous sacrifice while showing how betrayal and violence destroy the lovers.

### What are the main themes?

Love, sacrifice, jealousy, betrayal, night and daylight, and the transformation of tragedy into legend.

### What kind of poem is it?

It is a romantic narrative ballad with refrains, dialogue, vivid imagery, and varied galloping rhythms.

## References

- [Poetry Foundation](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poems/43187/the-highwayman)

- [Encyclopedia.com](https://www.encyclopedia.com/arts/educational-magazines/highwayman)

- [Penn State, ES Review](https://pure.psu.edu/en/publications/ballads-as-vessels-for-collective-cultural-memory-a-critical-comp/)

- [Poetry Foundation](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poems/43187/the-highwayman)

## Open the editor

Write with this poem’s rhythm in the editor: https://lyriic.com/write

# The Love Song of J. Alfred Prufrock analysis

The Love Song of J. Alfred Prufrock — T. S. Eliot (1915)

Eliot’s dramatic monologue turns social hesitation into a modernist study of self-consciousness, time, and failed connection.

Full text from [Prufrock and Other Observations](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Prufrock_and_Other_Observations/The_Love_Song_of_J._Alfred_Prufrock). Public domain in the US (First published in 1915, before the US public-domain cutoff.).

## Summary

Prufrock imagines an evening visit through streets and drawing rooms, but the proposed encounter never becomes decisive. His thoughts repeatedly return to appearance, age, and social judgment.

```
Let us go then, you and I,
When the evening is spread out against the sky
Like a patient etherized upon a table;
```

The poem ends in a sea fantasy where the mermaids sing to one another, not to Prufrock. Human voices wake the dreamer, and “we drown” closes the possibility of escape.[2]

## Meaning and interpretation

The poem presents paralysis as a condition of excessive interpretation. Prufrock can imagine “a hundred indecisions,” but every possible action is revised before it happens.[2]

```
And indeed there will be time
To wonder, "Do I dare?" and, "Do I dare?"
Time to turn back and descend the stair,
```

His alienation is social and inward: other people become eyes and formulas that pin him in place. The inability to say what he means becomes the poem’s central dramatic event.[3]

## Themes

### Indecision

Repeated questions turn a minor social risk into an existential crisis.

### Modern alienation

Urban streets, drawing rooms, and disconnected voices place people near one another without intimacy.[2]

### Time and aging

```
I have measured out my life with coffee spoons;
```

The image makes a life feel divided into small, repetitive rituals.

### Failed connection

Prufrock expects even revelation to be answered with misunderstanding, so speech cannot secure intimacy.

## Form and meter

This modernist dramatic monologue uses irregular free verse, short rhyming passages, refrains, dialogue, and abrupt shifts rather than one fixed meter.

Recurring lines such as “In the room the women come and go” create structure through echo and return. The poem’s form imitates thought that circles instead of arriving.

## Literary devices

### Simile

```
Like a patient etherized upon a table;
```

The opening image replaces a romantic evening with suspended consciousness, establishing paralysis immediately.

### Personification

```
The yellow fog that rubs its back upon the window-panes,
```

The catlike fog softens and encloses the city, mirroring Prufrock’s indirect movement.

### Repetition

```
In the room the women come and go
Talking of Michelangelo.
```

The refrain makes fashionable conversation feel cyclical and impersonal.

## Historical context

The poem appeared in Poetry in 1915 and in Prufrock and Other Observations in 1917. Its fractured voice and urban imagery make it an early English-language modernist landmark.

The Italian epigraph and allusions to Michelangelo, Hamlet, Lazarus, and John the Baptist place private anxiety inside a dense literary tradition.[3]

## What critics say

> “Prufrock’s dilemma is not that he is trapped but that he thinks that he knows that he is trapped.”
>
> — [Literary Theory and Criticism](https://literariness.org/2020/07/05/analysis-of-t-s-eliots-love-song-of-j-alfred-prufrock/)

> “The speaker in “The Love Song of J. Alfred Prufrock” is paralyzed by indecision.”
>
> — [LitCharts](https://www.litcharts.com/poetry/t-s-eliot/the-love-song-of-j-alfred-prufrock)

## Common questions

### What is the main meaning of Prufrock?

The poem explores how fear of judgment and self-consciousness prevent action and connection.

### What does “Do I dare?” mean?

It turns an unnamed social risk into a crisis, making hesitation the poem’s central action.

### What do the coffee spoons suggest?

They suggest a life measured by small, repetitive social rituals.

## References

- [Wikisource](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Prufrock_and_Other_Observations/The_Love_Song_of_J._Alfred_Prufrock)

- [Literary Theory and Criticism](https://literariness.org/2020/07/05/analysis-of-t-s-eliots-love-song-of-j-alfred-prufrock/)

- [LitCharts](https://www.litcharts.com/poetry/t-s-eliot/the-love-song-of-j-alfred-prufrock)

- [Wikisource](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Prufrock_and_Other_Observations/The_Love_Song_of_J._Alfred_Prufrock)

## Open the editor

Write with this poem’s open form in the editor: https://lyriic.com/write

# The Minstrel Boy analysis

The Minstrel Boy — Thomas Moore (1813)

Moore’s song joins military resistance to cultural resistance, making the harp as important as the sword.

Full text from [The Minstrel Boy](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/The_Minstrel_Boy). Public domain in the US (Published in 1813 as part of Irish Melodies, before the US public-domain cutoff.).

## Summary

A young minstrel goes to war with his father’s sword and his own harp. After he falls, he tears the harp’s strings rather than let the enemy make it sound in slavery.

```
The Minstrel-Boy to the war is gone,
In the ranks of death you'll find him;
His father's sword he has girded on,
```

The song presents artistic voice as part of national defense: the sword guards rights while the harp praises the land.[2]

## Meaning and interpretation

The harp symbolizes Ireland’s cultural identity, and its destruction is both tragic defeat and an act of agency. The oppressor can defeat the singer without making the instrument serve submission.[3]

```
The harp he lov'd ne'er spoke again,
For he tore its chords asunder;
And said, "No chains shall sully thee,
```

The final vow makes freedom the condition of authentic song rather than merely the minstrel’s political objective.[2]

## Themes

### Patriotism and sacrifice

The warrior-bard gives both body and art to a betrayed “Land of song.”

### Art and national identity

The harp carries communal identity alongside the sword.[3]

### Freedom versus slavery

```
Thy songs were made for the pure and free,
They shall never sound in slavery.
```

“Never” makes the ending a vow of refusal.

## Form and meter

This is a two-stanza narrative song in common-ballad movement, broadly alternating four- and three-stress lines.

Loose rhyme, emphatic punctuation, and a sudden dash after “The Minstrel fell!” make the song dramatic and performable.[2]

## Literary devices

### Symbolism

```
And his wild harp slung behind him.
```

The harp represents Irish music and cultural memory.

### Antithesis

```
One sword, at least, thy rights shall guard,
One faithful harp shall praise thee!
```

The parallel sword and harp give military and artistic resistance equal civic dignity.

### Repetition

```
One sword, at least...
One faithful harp shall praise thee!
```

Repeated “One” emphasizes loyalty when the wider world has betrayed the country.

## Historical context

Moore’s Irish Melodies appeared in the aftermath of the 1798 rebellion and the 1803 uprising associated with Robert Emmet. The song never names Ireland, but its harp and “Land of song” make the national context legible.[2]

Irish Music Daily describes the minstrel as an idealistic patriot rather than an experienced soldier.[3]

## What critics say

> “That the minstrel boy destroys his harp before it falls into enemy hands is tragic, as it signifies a knowing surrender of Irish freedom”
>
> — [Michael Mingo’s Blog](https://mgerardmingo.com/2018/06/29/thomas-moores-the-minstrel-boy-an-analysis/)

> “The very fact that he is a minstrel alerts us straightaway to the fact that he is not a soldier.”
>
> — [Irish Music Daily](https://www.irishmusicdaily.com/minstrel-boy-song-meaning)

## Common questions

### What is the meaning of The Minstrel Boy?

It presents artistic freedom and political freedom as inseparable forms of resistance.

### What does the harp symbolize?

The harp symbolizes Ireland’s musical culture and national identity.

### What is the form and meter?

It is a two-stanza narrative song using common-ballad movement and loose rhyme.

## References

- [Wikisource](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/The_Minstrel_Boy)

- [Michael Mingo’s Blog](https://mgerardmingo.com/2018/06/29/thomas-moores-the-minstrel-boy-an-analysis/)

- [Irish Music Daily](https://www.irishmusicdaily.com/minstrel-boy-song-meaning)

- [Michael Mingo’s Blog](https://mgerardmingo.com/2018/06/29/thomas-moores-the-minstrel-boy-an-analysis/)

## Open the editor

Write with this poem’s meter in the editor: https://lyriic.com/write/iambic-tetrameter

# The Rape of the Lock analysis

The Rape of the Lock — Alexander Pope (1714)

Pope turns a stolen lock of hair into a mock epic whose heroic couplets expose fashionable vanity and conflict.

Full text from [The Rape of the Lock and other poems](https://www.gutenberg.org/files/9800/9800-h/9800-h.htm). Public domain in the US (First published in 1712 and expanded in 1714, centuries before the US cutoff.).

## Summary

Belinda attends fashionable society, plays ombre, and becomes the target of the Baron, who cuts a lock of her hair. Sylphs guard her, but epic machinery cannot prevent the social crisis.

```
Swift to the Lock a thousand Sprites repair,
A thousand wings, by turns, blow back the hair;
And thrice they twitch'd the diamond in her ear;
```

The poem’s grand style makes a small social incident look enormous, revealing how status and reputation govern its world.[2]

## Meaning and interpretation

Its central joke is a mismatch between subject and style: cards, cosmetics, and scissors receive the language of war and epic destiny.[2]

```
Let Spades be trumps! she said, and trumps they were.
Now move to war her sable Matadores,
```

The satire is amused but not empty. The Baron’s language of conquest makes desire and possession visible beneath the comedy.[3]

## Themes

### Triviality and social importance

A lock is materially small but becomes a crisis of honor.

### Gender and possession

Epic battle language turns a fashionable flirtation into a contest over a woman’s body and reputation.

### Vanity and performance

Cards, fans, cosmetics, and conversation make identity a public performance.[3]

## Form and meter

The five-canto mock epic is chiefly written in heroic couplets: rhymed pairs of iambic pentameter.

Invocation, supernatural guardians, battle scenes, speeches, and elevated diction imitate epic conventions while miniaturizing them around fashionable life.[2]

## Literary devices

### Mock epic

```
And particolour'd troops, a shining train,
Draw forth to combat on the velvet plain.
```

The card table becomes a battlefield, creating comic disproportion.

### Bathos

```
Here Britain's statesmen oft the fall foredoom
Of foreign Tyrants and of Nymphs at home;
```

The movement from national politics to gossip deflates grandeur.

### Personification

```
T' inclose the Lock; now joins it, to divide.
```

The scissors become a heroic weapon in a miniature encounter.

## Historical context

Pope wrote the poem after a quarrel between Arabella Fermor and Lord Robert Petre. He published two cantos in 1712 and expanded the work to five in 1714.[3]

The early eighteenth-century setting includes Hampton Court, ombre, cosmetics, coffee, and elaborate dress, giving the satire a concrete social target.

## What critics say

> “Although Pope himself called the poem “An Heroi-Comical Poem,” critics like to call it a “mock epic.””
>
> — John L. Kessler, [eCampusOntario Pressbooks](https://ecampusontario.pressbooks.pub/lithumanities/chapter/chapter-6-pope-the-rape-of-the-lock/)

> “Pope's poem is a mock-heroic poem that treats a trivial subject in the elevated style of epic.”
>
> — [University of Virginia Literature in Context](https://anthology.lib.virginia.edu/work/Pope/pope-rape-lock)

## Common questions

### Why is it called a mock epic?

It imitates epic conventions while applying them to cards, cosmetics, gossip, and scissors.

### What is the main meaning?

The poem satirizes vanity, status anxiety, and possessive social conflict through comic disproportion.

### What form does it use?

It is a five-canto poem chiefly written in heroic couplets.

## References

- [Project Gutenberg](https://www.gutenberg.org/files/9800/9800-h/9800-h.htm)

- [John L. Kessler, eCampusOntario Pressbooks](https://ecampusontario.pressbooks.pub/lithumanities/chapter/chapter-6-pope-the-rape-of-the-lock/)

- [University of Virginia Literature in Context](https://anthology.lib.virginia.edu/work/Pope/pope-rape-lock)

- [Project Gutenberg](https://www.gutenberg.org/files/9800/9800-h/9800-h.htm)

## Open the editor

Write with this poem’s meter in the editor: https://lyriic.com/write/iambic-pentameter

# The Raven analysis

The Raven — Edgar Allan Poe (1845)

Poe’s tightly patterned narrative turns a grieving speaker’s questions into an escalating encounter with the word “Nevermore.”

Full text from [The Raven](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poems/48860/the-raven). Public domain in the US (First published in 1845, before the US public-domain cutoff.).

## Summary

On a bleak December night, a grieving speaker hears tapping, opens the window, and admits a raven. The bird perches above the chamber door and answers every question with one word.

```
Once upon a midnight dreary, while I pondered, weak and weary,
Over many a quaint and curious volume of forgotten lore—
```

The speaker gradually loads “Nevermore” with meanings about Lenore, relief, and the afterlife, until the bird becomes an image of permanent grief.[2]

## Meaning and interpretation

The poem presents grief as an interpretive loop. The bird may have learned one word from a former master, but the speaker supplies its increasingly painful meanings.[3]

```
Quoth the Raven “Nevermore.”
Much I marvelled this ungainly fowl to hear discourse so plainly,
```

By the final stanza, the refrain sounds less like an external prophecy than the speaker’s conclusion that sorrow will outlast him.[3]

## Themes

### Grief and memory

Books cannot provide “surcease of sorrow”; memory of Lenore keeps returning.

### Loss of hope

```
Is there—is there balm in Gilead?—tell me—tell me, I implore!
Quoth the Raven “Nevermore.”
```

Each question makes the repeated answer more final.

### Psychology and the supernatural

The raven can be supernatural, psychological, or both; its fixed word becomes terrifying through the speaker’s interpretation.

## Form and meter

The poem has eighteen six-line stanzas, traditionally using an ABCBBB rhyme pattern.

Its long lines are commonly described as trochaic octameter, varied by pauses, catalexis, internal rhyme, and shortened refrains.[2]

## Literary devices

### Internal rhyme

```
Once upon a midnight dreary, while I pondered, weak and weary,
```

Rhyme inside the line creates musical pressure before the end rhyme.

### Alliteration

```
While I nodded, nearly napping, suddenly there came a tapping,
```

Repeated consonants make the anxious scene audible.

### Refrain

```
Quoth the Raven “Nevermore.”
```

The same word changes meaning according to the speaker’s question.

## Historical context

Poe first published the poem in 1845 in The Raven and Other Poems. Its public-domain status permits short verse excerpts here.

Poe’s essay “The Philosophy of Composition” discusses melancholy, refrain, and intended unity of effect, though readers need not accept the essay as a complete account of composition.[3]

## What critics say

> ““The Raven” is a ballad utilizing trochaic octameter ... It also follows the ABCBBB rhyme scheme.”
>
> — LeDavid Olmstead, [University of Iowa Pressbooks](https://pressbooks.uiowa.edu/poetales/chapter/ledavid-olmstead-main-text/)

> “‘The Raven’ by Edgar Allan Poe is a ballad of eighteen six-line stanzas.”
>
> — [Poem Analysis](https://poemanalysis.com/edgar-allan-poe/the-raven/)

## Common questions

### What is the meaning of The Raven?

It shows a grieving speaker turning one repeated word into a verdict that loss and loneliness will never end.

### Who is Lenore?

Lenore is the speaker’s deceased beloved and the emotional center of his questions.

### What does Nevermore mean?

Its meaning grows from a learned word into the speaker’s imagined answer about grief, relief, and reunion.

## References

- [Poetry Foundation](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poems/48860/the-raven)

- [LeDavid Olmstead, University of Iowa Pressbooks](https://pressbooks.uiowa.edu/poetales/chapter/ledavid-olmstead-main-text/)

- [Poem Analysis](https://poemanalysis.com/edgar-allan-poe/the-raven/)

- [Poetry Foundation](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poems/48860/the-raven)

## Open the editor

Write with this poem’s meter in the editor: https://lyriic.com/write/trochaic-octameter
